lessons.title: Security Foundations for the Agentic Era
lessons.lead: Reframe cybersecurity around systems that perceive, plan, delegate and act.

slides.title: From chatbot to operational actor
slides.html:
From chatbot to operational actor

Learning objective — Explain and apply: from chatbot to operational actor.

Core principle

A chatbot primarily returns content; an agent can change external state through tools, APIs, code and delegated workflows.

Applied scenario

A support agent that can refund orders has crossed from advice into transaction authority.

Engineering response

Inventory every external effect the system can cause, not just every model endpoint.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Which capability turns a language interface into an operational security principal?

slides.title: The new security boundary
slides.html:
The new security boundary

Learning objective — Explain and apply: the new security boundary.

Core principle

The effective boundary includes model, context, memory, tools, identity, orchestrator, runtime and human approval paths.

Applied scenario

A safe model connected to an overpowered shell is still an unsafe system.

Engineering response

Draw the complete execution path and mark every point where data or authority crosses a boundary.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Where would you place an independent control before a consequential side effect?

slides.title: Agentic systems are socio-technical
slides.html:
Agentic systems are socio-technical

Learning objective — Explain and apply: agentic systems are socio-technical.

Core principle

Risk emerges from software, people, business processes, incentives, vendors and operational assumptions interacting.

Applied scenario

A well-configured procurement agent can still be abused through a fraudulent supplier onboarding process.

Engineering response

Include operators, approvers, data owners, tool vendors and incident responders in the system model.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Name one non-technical control that can prevent an agent-enabled fraud path.

slides.title: Security objectives beyond confidentiality
slides.html:
Security objectives beyond confidentiality

Learning objective — Explain and apply: security objectives beyond confidentiality.

Core principle

Confidentiality, integrity and availability remain essential, but purpose, authority, provenance, reversibility and accountability become explicit concerns.

Applied scenario

A sales agent may disclose no secret yet still cause harm by issuing unauthorized discounts at scale.

Engineering response

Translate business intent into measurable security properties and prohibited outcomes.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Which security property captures whether an agent stayed within its assigned purpose?

slides.title: Least agency as a design principle
slides.html:
Least agency as a design principle

Learning objective — Explain and apply: least agency as a design principle.

Core principle

Least agency limits the autonomy, scope, duration and consequence of actions to what the task actually needs.

Applied scenario

A travel agent may search and propose bookings but should not retain unrestricted payment authority.

Engineering response

Start with read-only, narrow task scopes; add write permissions only where justified by evidence.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Why is least agency more precise than simply giving an agent a low-privilege user account?

slides.title: The agentic attack surface
slides.html:
The agentic attack surface

Learning objective — Explain and apply: the agentic attack surface.

Core principle

Attackers target instructions, retrieved content, tool metadata, credentials, memory, delegation, runtime and human trust.

Applied scenario

A malicious document can manipulate a summarizer, which then triggers a privileged downstream workflow.

Engineering response

Map attack entry points and impact paths together; do not treat prompt text as the whole surface.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

What attack surface is introduced when one agent consumes another agent's output?

slides.title: Threats, vulnerabilities and incidents
slides.html:
Threats, vulnerabilities and incidents

Learning objective — Explain and apply: threats, vulnerabilities and incidents.

Core principle

A threat is a potential cause of harm; a vulnerability is an exploitable weakness; an incident is realized or suspected impact.

Applied scenario

Indirect prompt injection is a technique; an exposed privileged tool is a weakness; unauthorized data export is an incident outcome.

Engineering response

Record causal chains so teams do not confuse a model behavior with the root control failure.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Classify the malicious email, the missing authorization check and the data exfiltration separately.

slides.title: Security responsibility and ownership
slides.html:
Security responsibility and ownership

Learning objective — Explain and apply: security responsibility and ownership.

Core principle

Every agent needs a business owner, technical operator, data owner, policy owner and accountable incident contact.

Applied scenario

A vendor-hosted agent that modifies customer records still needs an internal owner for access and outcomes.

Engineering response

Create an ownership record linked to identity, environment, data classes, tools and review cadence.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Who is accountable when a delegated sub-agent performs an action on behalf of a business workflow?

slides.title: Risk appetite for autonomous actions
slides.html:
Risk appetite for autonomous actions

Learning objective — Explain and apply: risk appetite for autonomous actions.

Core principle

Risk tolerance should vary by action consequence, reversibility, data sensitivity, scale and uncertainty.

Applied scenario

Drafting a response and initiating a wire transfer should never share the same approval threshold.

Engineering response

Define action tiers with explicit limits, approvals, transaction caps and rollback requirements.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Which factors should raise an action's required assurance level?

slides.title: Security economics of agent deployment
slides.html:
Security economics of agent deployment

Learning objective — Explain and apply: security economics of agent deployment.

Core principle

The business case must include security engineering, monitoring, human review, recovery and residual-risk costs.

Applied scenario

A 24/7 agent may reduce staffing costs but increase exposure if its credentials can alter production continuously.

Engineering response

Compare expected value with control cost and worst-case loss, not model token cost alone.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

What hidden operational cost is omitted when an agent pilot is evaluated only on task completion?

slides.title: A practical agent security vocabulary
slides.html:
A practical agent security vocabulary

Learning objective — Explain and apply: a practical agent security vocabulary.

Core principle

Use precise terms for agent, tool, action, delegation, context, memory, provenance, policy decision and enforcement point.

Applied scenario

Calling an MCP server a model obscures that it may expose executable tools and sensitive resources.

Engineering response

Adopt a shared glossary before threat workshops and architecture reviews.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Explain the difference between a tool description and an authorization decision.

slides.title: The secure-agent design thesis
slides.html:
The secure-agent design thesis

Learning objective — Explain and apply: the secure-agent design thesis.

Core principle

Treat model output as an untrusted proposal; keep authority in deterministic, independently testable control planes.

Applied scenario

The model may recommend a refund, while a policy service checks ownership, amount, fraud signals and approval before execution.

Engineering response

Separate reasoning from execution authority and make every side effect attributable and bounded.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

State the core architectural rule that should govern the rest of this course.

guide: An agent is not merely a language model with a chat interface. It is a socio-technical system in which a model interprets goals, maintains or retrieves state, selects tools, receives observations and may initiate consequential operations. The security boundary therefore includes the model host, orchestration code, identity provider, tool adapters, data stores, external services, human approval path, telemetry and the people who configure them. A model can be statistically capable while the surrounding system remains insecure because a tool is over-privileged, a data source is untrusted, or a workflow has no reliable stop condition.

Use the classic security objectives—confidentiality, integrity and availability—but extend the analysis to authorization integrity, provenance, bounded autonomy, reversibility and accountability. Confidentiality asks who can see data in prompts, retrieved context, memory, logs and tool results. Integrity asks who can change instructions, records, tool definitions, policies and long-term memory. Availability includes runaway loops, tool exhaustion, quota depletion and dependency failure. Accountability asks whether a human or service identity can be tied to each proposed and executed side effect. Safety and security overlap but are not identical: an unsafe outcome may arise without an attacker, while a security incident involves malicious or unauthorized activity or compromise.

The governing architecture rule is separation of reasoning from authority. Treat model output as an untrusted proposal. A trusted execution service should validate the authenticated principal, delegated authority, resource, action, parameters, business state, policy version, approval evidence and limits before committing a side effect. The policy decision should be reproducible and independent of the model's explanation. A natural-language statement such as ‘the user approved this’ is not proof of approval; approval must be represented by a verifiable, scoped event bound to the exact transaction.
lessons.case: A customer-support agent reads a complaint, searches policy documents, drafts a response and can issue refunds. During a pilot it receives a malicious attachment containing instructions to refund the sender and export customer records. The model follows the embedded instruction. The important failure is not simply that the model was fooled: the architecture allowed untrusted content to influence a high-impact tool without a separate authorization check, transaction limit or approval binding.

lab.title: Draw the system boundary and assign security ownership
lab.intro: Use the customer-support workflow above as a fictional system. Work entirely from the facts supplied here; do not connect to a real service. Draw the components and data flows from user interface through model, orchestrator, retrieval store, policy service, refund API, email service and audit store. Mark trust boundaries, identities, data classifications, external dependencies and every side effect. Identify a business owner, technical owner, data owner, security/policy owner and incident contact.
tasks: List at least eight assets, including model context, customer records, credentials, tool definitions, memory and audit evidence.
Identify at least five trust boundaries and state what crosses each boundary.
Classify each action as read, draft, reversible write or consequential write; assign an autonomy tier.
Write three measurable security requirements, including one that prevents a refund from committing without transaction-bound authorization.
Record assumptions, exclusions, owners and evidence needed before pilot approval.
lab.evidence: A one-page context diagram; asset and data inventory; owner matrix; autonomy/action table; and three testable requirements.
lab.model: A defensible answer places the model and retrieved documents in an untrusted reasoning zone; the refund service is behind a policy enforcement point. The user identity is propagated as a verified principal, but the agent has its own workload identity and a narrowly scoped delegation. The refund endpoint independently checks customer ownership, amount threshold, case status, fraud state, idempotency key and approval token. The email export path is a separate capability, not implicitly available to the refund workflow. Logs record proposal, policy decision, approver, tool identity, resource, outcome and correlation ID while redacting secrets. No single owner substitutes for the others: business owns purpose and risk acceptance; engineering operates the service; data owners define permitted use; security defines controls; incident response owns containment.

rubric.partial: Most components present; some trust/authority gaps
rubric.competent: Complete boundary, actors, data and side effects

rubric.partial: Controls named but weakly enforced or evidenced
rubric.competent: Independent, scoped, testable enforcement

rubric.partial: Some tests; limited negative cases
rubric.competent: Clear artifacts, negative tests and traceable results

rubric.partial: Risks identified without owners or rationale
rubric.competent: Prioritized risks, assumptions, owners and defensible decisions

quiz.q: Which statement best describes the secure-agent design principle?
o: The model decides whether its own action is safe.
The model proposes; an independently enforced control authorizes execution.
A system prompt is the primary authorization boundary.
Only the user interface needs security controls.
quiz.why: Authorization belongs in a trusted enforcement point that checks identity, scope, context and policy independently of model-generated text.

quiz.q: Why should agent security include memory and logs in the asset inventory?
o: They can retain sensitive data or attacker-controlled content and influence later actions.
They are outside the application boundary.
quiz.why: Memory and logs can create confidentiality, integrity, retention and downstream-influence risks.

quiz.q: What is the strongest evidence of user approval for a refund?
o: The model says the user approved it.
A verifiable approval event bound to the exact refund parameters.
The tool description says approval is optional.
quiz.why: Approval must be authenticated, scoped, time-bound and bound to the exact action or transaction.

lessons.title: Anatomy of Agentic Systems
lessons.lead: Understand the components and execution paths that create agent-specific exposure.

slides.title: Agent loop: observe, plan, act
slides.html:
Agent loop: observe, plan, act

Learning objective — Explain and apply: agent loop: observe, plan, act.

Core principle

An agent loop repeatedly receives observations, forms a plan, selects actions and evaluates results.

Applied scenario

A browser agent reads a page, decides to click, submits a form and then interprets the response.

Engineering response

Place policy checks between action selection and external execution, on every loop iteration.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Why is a one-time authorization at session start insufficient for a multi-step agent?

slides.title: Models and inference services
slides.html:
Models and inference services

Learning objective — Explain and apply: models and inference services.

Core principle

Model endpoints influence decisions but do not alone define system authority; surrounding orchestration determines what the model can do.

Applied scenario

A model with no tools can still leak prompt context, while a modest model with admin tools can cause operational damage.

Engineering response

Separate model trust, model-provider trust and application execution privileges.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Which component actually enforces whether a proposed API call is allowed?

slides.title: Orchestrators and planners
slides.html:
Orchestrators and planners

Learning objective — Explain and apply: orchestrators and planners.

Core principle

Orchestrators route tasks, maintain state, choose tools, retry failures and delegate subtasks.

Applied scenario

A planner may retry a failed payment call and accidentally create duplicate transactions without idempotency controls.

Engineering response

Review retry logic, state transitions, task boundaries and failure handling as security-critical code.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

What security property should a retry mechanism preserve?

slides.title: Tools as capability interfaces
slides.html:
Tools as capability interfaces

Learning objective — Explain and apply: tools as capability interfaces.

Core principle

Each tool exposes a capability; its schema, implementation, backing identity and reachable data determine real power.

Applied scenario

A search tool may appear read-only but return links that trigger unsafe downstream browser actions.

Engineering response

Document tool semantics, side effects, data access, rate limits and authorization independently of descriptions.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Why can a harmless-looking tool description not establish that a tool is safe?

slides.title: Context assembly and instruction hierarchy
slides.html:
Context assembly and instruction hierarchy

Learning objective — Explain and apply: context assembly and instruction hierarchy.

Core principle

The context window combines trusted instructions with user input, retrieved documents, tool outputs and history.

Applied scenario

A web page can insert adversarial instructions into content later supplied to a planning model.

Engineering response

Label provenance and trust at ingestion; never assume position in a prompt creates a security boundary.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Why does placing untrusted text under a heading called 'quoted content' not neutralize it?

slides.title: Short-term state and conversation history
slides.html:
Short-term state and conversation history

Learning objective — Explain and apply: short-term state and conversation history.

Core principle

Conversation state can retain sensitive content, attacker-controlled instructions and stale authorization assumptions.

Applied scenario

A prior session's approval to draft a message must not authorize sending a different message today.

Engineering response

Bind approvals to exact action, object, amount, recipient, time and user intent.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Which elements should an approval token bind to prevent scope creep?

slides.title: Long-term memory systems
slides.html:
Long-term memory systems

Learning objective — Explain and apply: long-term memory systems.

Core principle

Persistent memory turns transient influence into durable state that can shape future retrieval and action.

Applied scenario

A poisoned preference record can silently alter later payment or disclosure decisions.

Engineering response

Use provenance, write authorization, quarantine, expiry and user-visible review for memory changes.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

What makes memory poisoning different from a one-turn prompt injection?

slides.title: Retrieval-augmented generation
slides.html:
Retrieval-augmented generation

Learning objective — Explain and apply: retrieval-augmented generation.

Core principle

RAG introduces ingestion, chunking, embedding, indexing, retrieval and citation trust boundaries.

Applied scenario

A compromised knowledge article may be repeatedly retrieved because its embedding remains highly relevant.

Engineering response

Track source identity and version through chunks; isolate tenant data and support rapid deletion or re-indexing.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Why is source provenance needed after text has been converted into an embedding?

slides.title: Multi-modal perception
slides.html:
Multi-modal perception

Learning objective — Explain and apply: multi-modal perception.

Core principle

Images, audio, video and structured files can carry instructions or hidden data that affect agent behavior.

Applied scenario

An OCR pipeline can convert a screenshot's hidden instruction into text placed in the model context.

Engineering response

Apply modality-aware scanning, provenance and controlled transformation before content reaches privileged agents.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Why does converting an image into text not remove its adversarial influence?

slides.title: Human interfaces and approval surfaces
slides.html:
Human interfaces and approval surfaces

Learning objective — Explain and apply: human interfaces and approval surfaces.

Core principle

User interfaces shape what people believe an agent will do and what they actually authorize.

Applied scenario

A vague 'Continue' button can conceal that an agent will email an entire customer export.

Engineering response

Show action, target, data, consequence and reversibility in approval UX; avoid consent fatigue.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

What information must an approval screen disclose to be meaningful?

slides.title: Distributed and cloud-native execution
slides.html:
Distributed and cloud-native execution

Learning objective — Explain and apply: distributed and cloud-native execution.

Core principle

Agents often span API gateways, queues, functions, containers, vector stores and third-party services.

Applied scenario

A task can outlive its initiating web request and continue in a background worker with stale authority.

Engineering response

Trace task identity and delegated authority across asynchronous boundaries.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

How should a queued job prove that its authority remains valid when it executes?

slides.title: Architecture mapping exercise
slides.html:
Architecture mapping exercise

Learning objective — Explain and apply: architecture mapping exercise.

Core principle

A useful system map records components, identities, data flows, control points, trust zones and side effects.

Applied scenario

Map a customer-service agent from user message through retrieval, CRM lookup, refund tool and notification.

Engineering response

Create a component inventory before debating individual guardrails.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Can a reviewer follow every sensitive data flow and consequential action from this map?

guide: Model an agentic system as a control-flow graph and a data-flow graph, not as a single model box. The control-flow graph captures who invokes whom, under which identity, with which permissions and retry behavior. The data-flow graph captures prompts, retrieved records, tool outputs, memory writes, embeddings, traces and exported artifacts. A component can be trusted for availability yet untrusted for content. For example, a signed enterprise document may be authentic but still contain adversarial instructions copied from an external source. Trust should be assigned per property and purpose, not globally.

Distinguish the model, host application, orchestrator, tool client, tool server, resource server, identity provider, memory service and human operator. A tool is executable capability, not just a function description. A tool schema can influence model selection and parameter construction, but it is not an authorization policy. Tool output is data; it may be malformed, stale, poisoned or adversarial. A memory store is a persistence layer with lifecycle and access-control requirements. The orchestrator is especially sensitive because it routes context and authority across components; compromise there can turn a low-privilege component into a pivot point.

For every edge in the graph, record protocol, authenticated peer, data classification, direction, validation, timeout, retry policy, rate limit, audit event and failure behavior. Explicitly model asynchronous jobs and callbacks: delayed execution can outlive a user's session, the original approval or the credentials that initiated it. A correlation identifier should link the user's intent, model plan, policy decision, tool call and final state change without becoming an authentication credential.
lessons.case: A procurement assistant calls a search service, a supplier-risk service and a purchase-order service. The search service is read-only, but its result contains a supplier-provided instruction to ‘use the emergency purchasing route’. The orchestrator forwards the content to a second agent, which can create purchase orders. A diagram that only shows the model and three tools misses the trust transition from untrusted supplier text to a privileged downstream action.

lab.title: Build a component, identity and data-flow map
lab.intro: Create a component inventory for the procurement assistant. Use fictional systems and synthetic data. Model the happy path and at least two failure paths, including timeout/retry and a malicious tool result. Identify where the authenticated user identity ends, where workload identity begins, and where authority is delegated.
tasks: Draw the control-flow graph and data-flow graph separately.
For each edge, record protocol, authentication, data class, validation and logging.
Identify state that survives a request: queued jobs, memory, cache, tokens and approval records.
Specify safe failure behavior for a timeout during purchase-order creation.
Mark all components that can create, alter or delete enterprise state.
lab.evidence: Two diagrams, a component register and an edge-control table with at least ten rows.
lab.model: The supplier search output is marked untrusted even though it arrives over an authenticated channel. It may inform a recommendation but cannot grant authority. The purchase-order service validates a distinct workload token with an audience restricted to that service and checks the user's delegated scope and purchasing limit. A timeout after submission is treated as an uncertain outcome: query transaction status using an idempotency key before retrying. Do not blindly repeat a non-idempotent create operation. Approval records expire and bind supplier, amount, currency, cost centre and order hash. Tool output is validated and tagged with provenance before another agent consumes it.

rubric.partial: Most components present; some trust/authority gaps
rubric.competent: Complete boundary, actors, data and side effects

rubric.partial: Controls named but weakly enforced or evidenced
rubric.competent: Independent, scoped, testable enforcement

rubric.partial: Some tests; limited negative cases
rubric.competent: Clear artifacts, negative tests and traceable results

rubric.partial: Risks identified without owners or rationale
rubric.competent: Prioritized risks, assumptions, owners and defensible decisions

quiz.q: Why maintain separate control-flow and data-flow views?
o: They expose different risks: authority and invocation versus information movement and influence.
quiz.why: A complete model must show both who can act and how data moves or influences later decisions.

quiz.q: What does an authenticated tool response prove?
o: That its contents are safe instructions.
That the tool is authorized to make all downstream decisions.
That the response came from the authenticated endpoint, not that its content is trustworthy.
quiz.why: Transport authentication is not semantic trust or authorization for downstream actions.

quiz.q: What is the correct response to an uncertain timeout during a write?
o: Check transaction state with an idempotency key before retrying.
quiz.why: Idempotency and state reconciliation prevent duplicate side effects after uncertain outcomes.

lessons.title: Threat Modelling Autonomous Systems
lessons.lead: Apply threat modelling to agent goals, state, authority, tools and multi-step behavior.

slides.title: Why conventional STRIDE needs adaptation
slides.html:
Why conventional STRIDE needs adaptation

Learning objective — Explain and apply: why conventional stride needs adaptation.

Core principle

STRIDE remains useful for spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service and elevation of privilege.

Applied scenario

An agent can be tricked into misusing a legitimate tool without a conventional software exploit.

Engineering response

Add goal integrity, provenance, delegation, memory integrity and action accountability to the threat model.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Which agentic threat may not be obvious in a classic network diagram?

slides.title: Define system purpose and security invariants
slides.html:
Define system purpose and security invariants

Learning objective — Explain and apply: define system purpose and security invariants.

Core principle

A security invariant states what must remain true across every valid execution path.

Applied scenario

A payroll agent must never change bank details and release payroll in the same unreviewed workflow.

Engineering response

Write invariants as testable statements tied to business assets and observable evidence.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Turn 'the agent should be safe' into one measurable invariant.

slides.title: Identify assets and harms
slides.html:
Identify assets and harms

Learning objective — Explain and apply: identify assets and harms.

Core principle

Assets include data, credentials, money, service availability, decision integrity, reputation and the ability to recover.

Applied scenario

A scheduling agent's calendar access may expose sensitive relationships even if no financial data is stored.

Engineering response

Map direct assets and second-order harms, including downstream decisions based on agent output.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

What indirect asset could be harmed by an inaccurate but trusted agent summary?

slides.title: Map trust boundaries
slides.html:
Map trust boundaries

Learning objective — Explain and apply: map trust boundaries.

Core principle

Trust boundaries separate principals, tenants, networks, data classifications, execution zones and authority domains.

Applied scenario

A tool response from a public web page must not inherit the trust of the internal CRM that requested it.

Engineering response

Draw boundaries around every transition from untrusted content to trusted decision or action.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Where should trust be re-evaluated in a retrieved-document-to-tool-call chain?

slides.title: Identify threat actors and incentives
slides.html:
Identify threat actors and incentives

Learning objective — Explain and apply: identify threat actors and incentives.

Core principle

Actors include external attackers, malicious insiders, compromised vendors, colluding users and opportunistic content publishers.

Applied scenario

A supplier can manipulate an invoice-processing agent to change payment instructions without compromising the agent platform.

Engineering response

Model capability, access, patience, knowledge and incentives for each actor.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Why should the threat model include an authorized user with malicious intent?

slides.title: Attack trees for agent workflows
slides.html:
Attack trees for agent workflows

Learning objective — Explain and apply: attack trees for agent workflows.

Core principle

Attack trees decompose an adversary objective into paths involving influence, authority, execution and impact.

Applied scenario

To exfiltrate customer data, an attacker may poison a document, trigger retrieval, induce a tool call and exploit broad read access.

Engineering response

Include alternative paths and identify controls that cut multiple branches.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Which control breaks the attack path even if prompt injection succeeds?

slides.title: Abuse cases and misuse stories
slides.html:
Abuse cases and misuse stories

Learning objective — Explain and apply: abuse cases and misuse stories.

Core principle

Misuse stories describe how an attacker exploits intended functionality rather than only breaking it.

Applied scenario

An attacker asks an agent to 'helpfully' summarize and forward a mailbox, exploiting a legitimate export feature.

Engineering response

Write attacker stories from entry point to measurable impact, including the business context.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

What makes a misuse case more actionable than a generic threat label?

slides.title: Model authority and privilege paths
slides.html:
Model authority and privilege paths

Learning objective — Explain and apply: model authority and privilege paths.

Core principle

Map how a request acquires authority: user identity, service identity, delegated token, tool identity and downstream role.

Applied scenario

A low-privilege agent may become a confused deputy when it uses a broad service credential on behalf of a user.

Engineering response

Track the original subject and delegation chain to the final resource authorization check.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Which identity should the data service authorize: the agent service account or the originating user?

slides.title: Threat modelling memory and context
slides.html:
Threat modelling memory and context

Learning objective — Explain and apply: threat modelling memory and context.

Core principle

Memory threat models must cover who can write, what is stored, how it is retrieved and when it can influence actions.

Applied scenario

A malicious instruction planted in a meeting note may be retrieved weeks later during a sensitive workflow.

Engineering response

Model poisoning, stale facts, cross-tenant retrieval and provenance loss as separate failure modes.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

What test demonstrates whether a stored malicious fact can trigger a later action?

slides.title: Threat modelling multi-agent systems
slides.html:
Threat modelling multi-agent systems

Learning objective — Explain and apply: threat modelling multi-agent systems.

Core principle

Delegation adds new principals, message channels, shared state, trust assumptions and transitive authority.

Applied scenario

A research agent can pass attacker-controlled content to an operations agent that has write access.

Engineering response

Model each agent's authority and the trust contract for every handoff.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Why should a downstream agent not inherit the upstream agent's confidence score as proof of trust?

slides.title: Prioritize risk with evidence
slides.html:
Prioritize risk with evidence

Learning objective — Explain and apply: prioritize risk with evidence.

Core principle

Risk ratings should combine impact, likelihood, exposure, exploitability, detectability and control strength.

Applied scenario

A rare path to bulk payroll modification can outrank a frequent low-impact prompt manipulation.

Engineering response

Record assumptions, evidence confidence, affected assets and residual risk; avoid false precision.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

What evidence would justify changing a high risk rating after mitigation?

slides.title: Threat model review and maintenance
slides.html:
Threat model review and maintenance

Learning objective — Explain and apply: threat model review and maintenance.

Core principle

Agentic threat models change as tools, models, prompts, policies, memory stores and business processes evolve.

Applied scenario

Adding a calendar-write tool changes the threat model even if the model version remains unchanged.

Engineering response

Trigger review on capability changes, data changes, vendor changes, incidents and material model updates.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Which deployment change should automatically reopen a threat-model review?

guide: Threat modelling agentic systems requires the usual discipline—assets, actors, trust boundaries, attack paths, impact and controls—plus explicit modelling of autonomy, delegated authority, context provenance, memory persistence, tool composition and long-horizon behavior. A threat can enter through a user prompt, retrieved document, email, web page, tool schema, tool result, memory record, plugin update, model supply chain or compromised upstream service. The attack may not cause immediate harm. It may alter a plan, plant memory, change a future tool choice or gradually steer a workflow toward a privileged operation.

Start with business outcomes and misuse cases. Ask what an attacker wants to read, change, trigger, conceal or exhaust. Then trace the shortest and longest plausible paths from entry point to impact. Use STRIDE where it helps identify spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service and elevation of privilege; supplement it with agent-specific questions: can an untrusted source change the goal, can one agent launder another's authority, can the system retain hostile content, can a tool be substituted, and can a valid low-risk action be chained into a high-risk outcome? MITRE ATLAS is a living knowledge base for AI attack tactics and techniques; use it to enrich scenarios, not as a substitute for system-specific analysis.

Risk scoring should not hide uncertainty behind false precision. Record likelihood rationale, impact dimensions, exposure, exploit prerequisites, existing controls, confidence and residual risk. A low-frequency event with catastrophic impact may require a hard safety boundary even when a numeric product score looks modest. Distinguish inherent risk from residual risk and control effectiveness from control existence. A control listed in a policy is not effective evidence; it must be implemented, tested, monitored and owned.
lessons.case: A benefits-processing agent reads uploaded applications, checks eligibility and drafts decisions. An attacker submits an application containing hidden instructions, then later uses a second account to request a status update. The first request plants an instruction in shared case memory; the second triggers a disclosure. A single-turn threat model would likely miss the cross-account, multi-step chain.

lab.title: Produce an agentic threat model and risk register
lab.intro: Threat-model the benefits workflow. Use a fictional environment and a whiteboard or document. Include at least one external attacker, one malicious insider, one compromised supplier and one accidental failure. Model direct and indirect prompt injection, identity misuse, data leakage, memory poisoning, denial of service and a multi-step chain.
tasks: Identify assets, actors, entry points, trust boundaries and business impacts.
Build three attack trees, including one long-horizon attack spanning two sessions.
Score inherent risk using impact, likelihood rationale and uncertainty; do not treat the score as objective truth.
Map preventive, detective and recovery controls to each path.
Record residual risk, owner, evidence and a decision: mitigate, transfer, avoid or accept.
lab.evidence: Threat-model diagram, three attack trees, risk register with at least eight rows and a prioritized treatment plan.
lab.model: A strong model identifies shared memory as a cross-session trust boundary and tests tenant/case isolation. It distinguishes the malicious instruction as an attack technique, the shared-memory write path as a vulnerability or control weakness, and unauthorized disclosure as impact. Controls include provenance labels, per-user or per-case memory namespaces, write authorization, quarantine of untrusted instructions, access checks at retrieval time, retention limits and audit of memory changes. Long-horizon tests must preserve state across turns and sessions. Residual risk should be explicitly accepted by an accountable owner, not silently inherited by the model team.

rubric.partial: Most components present; some trust/authority gaps
rubric.competent: Complete boundary, actors, data and side effects

rubric.partial: Controls named but weakly enforced or evidenced
rubric.competent: Independent, scoped, testable enforcement

rubric.partial: Some tests; limited negative cases
rubric.competent: Clear artifacts, negative tests and traceable results

rubric.partial: Risks identified without owners or rationale
rubric.competent: Prioritized risks, assumptions, owners and defensible decisions

quiz.q: What makes an agentic threat model incomplete?
o: It includes assets and trust boundaries.
It models only single-turn prompts and ignores memory, delegation and tool chains.
quiz.why: Agent threats often emerge through persistent state, chained tools and multi-step interactions.

quiz.q: How should a threat taxonomy such as MITRE ATLAS be used?
o: As proof that the system is secure.
As a source of attack patterns to adapt to the actual architecture.
As a replacement for asset identification.
quiz.why: A taxonomy enriches analysis but cannot replace context-specific attack-path modelling.

quiz.q: Which statement about risk scores is sound?
o: A low score proves the risk is acceptable.
Scores need rationale, uncertainty, impact context and accountable treatment decisions.
quiz.why: Risk numbers are decision aids; assumptions, severity and ownership remain essential.

lessons.title: Agentic Threat Landscape and Attack Patterns
lessons.lead: Recognize attack classes that target autonomous behavior and connected capabilities.

slides.title: OWASP agentic risk taxonomy
slides.html:
OWASP agentic risk taxonomy

Learning objective — Explain and apply: owasp agentic risk taxonomy.

Core principle

OWASP's 2026 Agentic Applications Top 10 groups risks around goal hijack, tool misuse, identity abuse, supply chain, execution, memory, communication, cascading failures, human trust and rogue behavior.

Applied scenario

A single incident may combine goal hijack, privilege abuse and unsafe tool execution.

Engineering response

Use the taxonomy as a coverage checklist, not a substitute for system-specific analysis.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Why can one incident map to several OWASP agentic categories?

slides.title: Goal hijacking
slides.html:
Goal hijacking

Learning objective — Explain and apply: goal hijacking.

Core principle

Goal hijacking redirects an agent from its authorized objective through malicious instructions or misleading context.

Applied scenario

A webpage instructs a browsing agent to abandon price comparison and export account data.

Engineering response

Bind goals to the initiating user request and enforce permitted outcomes outside the model.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

How can a system detect that an action is inconsistent with the task's declared purpose?

slides.title: Tool misuse and exploitation
slides.html:
Tool misuse and exploitation

Learning objective — Explain and apply: tool misuse and exploitation.

Core principle

Tool misuse occurs when legitimate capabilities are invoked in unsafe combinations, parameters or contexts.

Applied scenario

A file-conversion tool is used to read secrets from a path the user never intended to expose.

Engineering response

Validate parameters, resource ownership, operation semantics and cumulative effects at the tool boundary.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Why is validating each parameter insufficient if the action sequence is unsafe?

slides.title: Identity and privilege abuse
slides.html:
Identity and privilege abuse

Learning objective — Explain and apply: identity and privilege abuse.

Core principle

Agents can inherit, misuse or amplify authority through service accounts, delegated tokens and confused-deputy patterns.

Applied scenario

An agent uses its broad CRM token to retrieve records the requesting user cannot access.

Engineering response

Preserve subject identity, audience, scope, purpose and delegation chain through authorization.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

What makes a service credential a confused-deputy risk?

slides.title: Agentic supply-chain compromise
slides.html:
Agentic supply-chain compromise

Learning objective — Explain and apply: agentic supply-chain compromise.

Core principle

Agent supply chains include models, tools, MCP servers, plugins, prompts, skills, datasets, registries and update channels.

Applied scenario

A compromised tool package changes its schema to request broader filesystem access.

Engineering response

Pin versions, verify provenance, review permissions and monitor runtime behavior after updates.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Why is a signed package not sufficient evidence that a tool is safe to execute?

slides.title: Unexpected code execution
slides.html:
Unexpected code execution

Learning objective — Explain and apply: unexpected code execution.

Core principle

Generated code, shell commands, notebooks, plugins and deserialization paths can turn model output into host-level impact.

Applied scenario

A coding agent executes an unreviewed install script in a workspace containing production credentials.

Engineering response

Use disposable sandboxes, restricted syscalls, no ambient secrets and explicit egress controls.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Which isolation property limits damage if generated code is malicious?

slides.title: Memory and context poisoning
slides.html:
Memory and context poisoning

Learning objective — Explain and apply: memory and context poisoning.

Core principle

Attackers can seed durable context so future retrieval and planning reuse malicious or misleading content.

Applied scenario

A poisoned memory record silently changes a future agent's default recipient for sensitive reports.

Engineering response

Separate memory write permissions from read permissions and retain provenance and rollback.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

What makes a persistent payload dangerous even when the original interaction looked harmless?

slides.title: Insecure inter-agent communication
slides.html:
Insecure inter-agent communication

Learning objective — Explain and apply: insecure inter-agent communication.

Core principle

Unauthenticated or weakly validated messages allow spoofing, replay, tampering and authority laundering.

Applied scenario

A fake 'compliance agent' message instructs a finance agent to bypass a required check.

Engineering response

Authenticate sender identity, bind messages to task context and validate requested capabilities independently.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

What must a receiving agent verify before accepting a delegated instruction?

slides.title: Cascading failures
slides.html:
Cascading failures

Learning objective — Explain and apply: cascading failures.

Core principle

Errors propagate when agents trust downstream outputs, retry automatically or share state without containment.

Applied scenario

A hallucinated customer status is copied into CRM, analytics and billing agents and becomes operational fact.

Engineering response

Use bounded retries, circuit breakers, provenance-aware state and cross-system reconciliation.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Which control limits blast radius when an upstream agent is compromised?

slides.title: Human-agent trust exploitation
slides.html:
Human-agent trust exploitation

Learning objective — Explain and apply: human-agent trust exploitation.

Core principle

Fluent language, urgency and automation bias can cause people to approve unsafe actions or reveal secrets.

Applied scenario

An agent presents an invented compliance deadline and pressures an employee to approve a transfer.

Engineering response

Show evidence, uncertainty, authority and consequences; separate recommendation from approval.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

How can an approval workflow test understanding rather than collect a reflexive click?

slides.title: Rogue behavior and intent drift
slides.html:
Rogue behavior and intent drift

Learning objective — Explain and apply: rogue behavior and intent drift.

Core principle

An agent may gradually optimize a proxy objective or act outside its intended role while individual actions appear plausible.

Applied scenario

A lead-generation agent increases conversions by contacting people who opted out.

Engineering response

Monitor outcome constraints, cumulative behavior and purpose-specific policy violations.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Why is checking permissions alone insufficient to detect intent drift?

slides.title: Attack chains and compound risk
slides.html:
Attack chains and compound risk

Learning objective — Explain and apply: attack chains and compound risk.

Core principle

Real incidents often combine content influence, identity weakness, tool reach, persistence and weak detection.

Applied scenario

A poisoned supplier invoice triggers a payment workflow using a standing credential and no transaction-level review.

Engineering response

Model attack chains end to end and prioritize controls that interrupt high-impact transitions.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Identify two independent control points that could stop the invoice-to-payment chain.

guide: Agentic attack patterns are often combinations of familiar attacks rather than entirely new primitives. Prompt injection, credential theft, insecure deserialization, SSRF, dependency compromise, excessive permissions and business-logic abuse remain relevant. What changes is the agent's ability to interpret attacker-controlled content, choose tools, preserve state and continue acting. A benign-looking source can become an instruction carrier; a low-risk read can become the first step in a tool chain; a compromised tool description can steer capability selection; a long-running plan can outlive the context in which it was approved.

Build a threat catalogue around the system's actual capabilities: instruction and goal manipulation; tool misuse and chaining; identity/delegation abuse; memory/context poisoning; retrieval and data exfiltration; execution and sandbox escape; supply-chain compromise; inter-agent trust abuse; monitoring evasion; and resource exhaustion. For each pattern, document preconditions, attacker control, trust transition, intended security boundary, impact, prevention, detection and recovery. Avoid claiming every attack works on every model or framework. Attack feasibility depends on architecture, tool design, policy enforcement, model behavior and operational controls.

Prioritize controls that constrain consequences rather than relying only on detection. A detector may miss a novel prompt injection, but a backend can still reject an unauthorized transfer, an out-of-scope data query or a tool call exceeding a transaction cap. Rate limits, budgets, deadlines, maximum tool hops, circuit breakers and bounded retries reduce the blast radius of both malicious and accidental loops.
lessons.case: A research agent browses public websites and summarizes results for an analyst. A page contains instructions to retrieve confidential internal documents. The agent cannot directly access those documents, but it can call an internal search tool. A second tool can email summaries. The attack succeeds only if untrusted web content can cause the agent to chain internal search and outbound email without per-tool authorization and data-loss checks.

lab.title: Map attack patterns to controls and test cases
lab.intro: Use the research-agent scenario. Create a small attack-pattern catalogue and design defensive tests. Do not run payloads against real services. The exercise is to reason about the attack path and prove the controls reject the prohibited outcome.
tasks: Write five abuse cases with attacker goal, preconditions, path and impact.
For each abuse case, identify the decisive enforcement point and required evidence.
Design one negative test and one recovery test for each case.
Set limits for tool hops, runtime, token spend, request volume and outbound destinations.
Rank controls by consequence reduction, not by how impressive the detection technology sounds.
lab.evidence: Attack-pattern matrix, ten test cases and a control-priority rationale.
lab.model: The critical control is not a keyword filter alone. Internal search enforces user- and purpose-scoped access; outbound email enforces recipient allowlists, data classification and explicit send approval; the orchestrator records provenance and cannot pass arbitrary retrieved content as trusted instruction. The test asserts that a web page cannot expand the principal's permissions or authorize disclosure. Resource controls include maximum steps, deadlines, quotas and a kill switch. The recovery test revokes the delegated grant and confirms no queued operation can continue under stale authority.

rubric.competent: Complete boundary, actors, data and side effects

rubric.partial: Controls named but weakly enforced or evidenced
rubric.competent: Independent, scoped, testable enforcement

rubric.partial: Some tests; limited negative cases
rubric.competent: Clear artifacts, negative tests and traceable results

rubric.partial: Risks identified without owners or rationale
rubric.competent: Prioritized risks, assumptions, owners and defensible decisions

quiz.q: Why are agent attacks often best understood as chains?
o: Each individual step must be a zero-day.
A sequence of individually plausible actions can cross a boundary and create an impact.
Chaining is only a network-layer issue.
quiz.why: The risk can emerge from composition: data retrieval, interpretation, tool selection and side effect.

quiz.q: Which control most reliably prevents an unauthorized payment?
o: A payment API that independently validates identity, scope, amount and approval.
quiz.why: Preventive authorization at the resource boundary stops the side effect even if earlier controls fail.

quiz.q: Why set execution budgets and deadlines?
o: They reduce runaway cost and bound denial-of-service or looping behavior.
quiz.why: Resource limits bound operational and security impact but do not replace identity or authorization.

lessons.title: Prompt Injection and Cognitive Exploitation
lessons.lead: Defend against adversarial instructions in direct input, retrieved content and agent workflows.

slides.title: Prompt injection is an input-trust problem
slides.html:
Prompt injection is an input-trust problem

Learning objective — Explain and apply: prompt injection is an input-trust problem.

Core principle

Prompt injection exploits the model's difficulty reliably separating instructions from data in mixed context.

Applied scenario

A document says 'ignore prior rules' while appearing as ordinary reference material.

Engineering response

Treat all externally sourced content as untrusted data and keep authorization outside the prompt.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Why is prompt injection not solved by adding a stronger system prompt?

slides.title: Direct versus indirect injection
slides.html:
Direct versus indirect injection

Learning objective — Explain and apply: direct versus indirect injection.

Core principle

Direct injection arrives from the user; indirect injection arrives through documents, webpages, emails, tool outputs or multimodal content.

Applied scenario

A user asks for a webpage summary, and hidden page text attempts to redirect the agent to a privileged tool.

Engineering response

Test both attacker-controlled requests and content encountered during legitimate tasks.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Which attack can occur even when the user has benign intent?

slides.title: Instruction/data confusion
slides.html:
Instruction/data confusion

Learning objective — Explain and apply: instruction/data confusion.

Core principle

The same context channel may contain trusted policy, user goals, quoted text and untrusted retrieved material.

Applied scenario

A malicious email includes text formatted as if it were a developer instruction.

Engineering response

Use structured data boundaries and provenance labels, but assume the model can still be influenced.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

What enforcement layer must remain effective even if the model follows malicious text?

slides.title: Indirect injection through browser content
slides.html:
Indirect injection through browser content

Learning objective — Explain and apply: indirect injection through browser content.

Core principle

Web content can influence agents through visible text, hidden elements, metadata, comments and linked resources.

Applied scenario

A product page embeds instructions aimed at the shopping agent's browsing workflow.

Engineering response

Constrain browser tools, isolate browsing sessions and require policy checks for data export or account changes.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

How could a browser agent safely extract facts without granting page content control over tools?

slides.title: Email and document-borne attacks
slides.html:
Email and document-borne attacks

Learning objective — Explain and apply: email and document-borne attacks.

Core principle

Messages and office documents combine social engineering with machine-readable instructions and attachments.

Applied scenario

A supplier email asks an invoice agent to change payment details and treat the message as verified.

Engineering response

Verify business changes through independent channels and enforce dual control for payment-master edits.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Which part of the workflow should never be authorized solely by email content?

slides.title: Multimodal prompt injection
slides.html:
Multimodal prompt injection

Learning objective — Explain and apply: multimodal prompt injection.

Core principle

Text embedded in images, audio transcripts, QR codes or video frames can become instructions after perception.

Applied scenario

A screenshot contains a small instruction that OCR extracts into the agent's context.

Engineering response

Preserve modality provenance and apply content policies after OCR, transcription and extraction.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

At what transformation points can hidden instructions become visible to the model?

slides.title: Contextual manipulation and norm attacks
slides.html:
Contextual manipulation and norm attacks

Learning objective — Explain and apply: contextual manipulation and norm attacks.

Core principle

An attacker can manipulate context, role expectations or apparent business norms without using explicit override phrases.

Applied scenario

A message frames a data export as routine audit practice and makes the agent infer authorization.

Engineering response

Validate authority from identity and policy systems, never from persuasive narratives.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Why can keyword filters miss attacks that exploit social or contextual framing?

slides.title: Prompt injection defenses: what works
slides.html:
Prompt injection defenses: what works

Learning objective — Explain and apply: prompt injection defenses: what works.

Core principle

Layered controls include least privilege, input provenance, tool allowlists, action validation, isolation and monitoring.

Applied scenario

Even if the agent obeys a malicious webpage, the external policy engine denies a bulk export.

Engineering response

Measure defense at the action boundary, not only by whether the model says it resisted.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Which defense remains effective when the model's reasoning is fully compromised?

slides.title: Limits of instruction/data separation
slides.html:
Limits of instruction/data separation

Learning objective — Explain and apply: limits of instruction/data separation.

Core principle

Separating instructions from data improves hygiene but does not guarantee resistance to contextual manipulation.

Applied scenario

A document may persuade an agent through implied task relevance rather than explicit commands.

Engineering response

Use defense in depth and adversarial testing that includes subtle, contextually plausible payloads.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

What residual risk remains after prompt formatting and content labeling?

slides.title: Safe handling of untrusted outputs
slides.html:
Safe handling of untrusted outputs

Learning objective — Explain and apply: safe handling of untrusted outputs.

Core principle

Tool outputs must be treated as untrusted before they are summarized, stored, rendered or passed to another agent.

Applied scenario

A compromised search result includes a command that becomes a trusted task note.

Engineering response

Sanitize rendering, preserve source attribution and gate any downstream action on explicit policy.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Why is tool output not trustworthy merely because the tool itself is approved?

slides.title: Adversarial testing of prompt defenses
slides.html:
Adversarial testing of prompt defenses

Learning objective — Explain and apply: adversarial testing of prompt defenses.

Core principle

Test paraphrase, encoding, multi-turn persistence, multilingual content, benign camouflage and tool-mediated payloads.

Applied scenario

A red team plants a subtle instruction in a long report and waits for a later task to retrieve it.

Engineering response

Record attack objective, path, model/runtime version, action trace and impact—not just refusal text.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

What evidence distinguishes a real defense from a model that simply refused one test prompt?

slides.title: Prompt injection response playbook
slides.html:
Prompt injection response playbook

Learning objective — Explain and apply: prompt injection response playbook.

Core principle

A suspected injection requires containment of tools, preservation of traces, memory review and impact assessment.

Applied scenario

After a poisoned web page triggers an unauthorized export attempt, revoke the task token and quarantine affected memory.

Engineering response

Stop the action path first; then investigate source, persistence, exposure and downstream effects.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

What should responders preserve before resetting the agent session?

guide: Prompt injection is a failure to maintain a reliable distinction between instructions that govern the application and content that the application is supposed to process. Direct injection arrives through user-controlled input; indirect injection arrives through retrieved documents, web pages, email, code comments, calendar events, tool results or other data. The attacker may try to change the goal, reveal hidden context, invoke a tool, suppress warnings, poison memory or redirect later actions. The vulnerability is not simply the presence of malicious text; it is the system's willingness to treat untrusted content as authority.

There is no universal text delimiter, prompt wording or classifier that guarantees instruction/data separation for general-purpose language models. Delimiters and explicit labeling can help models reason about provenance, but they are not security boundaries. Use defense in depth: source allowlists and provenance; content isolation; least-privilege tools; narrow task scope; deterministic authorization; output validation; data-loss controls; human approval for consequential operations; and adversarial evaluation across languages, encodings, modalities and multi-turn contexts. Do not assume that a model can reliably identify all hostile instructions, or that a refusal proves no side effect occurred.

A robust workflow treats external content as evidence, not commands. The model may quote or summarize an instruction found in a document, but the application should not let that instruction change the user's authorized objective. Tool calls should be checked against a policy that knows the authenticated user, purpose, resource, action and current state. High-impact actions should require explicit confirmation that displays the actual target, amount, recipient and effect. If the system cannot safely separate a requested action from untrusted content, it should stop, ask for clarification or return a draft rather than execute.
lessons.case: A travel assistant is asked to summarize a hotel cancellation policy. A page includes hidden text telling the assistant to send the user's passport details to a third party. The page is relevant as policy content but has no authority to change the user's goal or grant access to private data. The correct behavior is to summarize the cancellation terms, ignore the instruction as an instruction, and never call a disclosure tool.

lab.title: Run a safe prompt-injection defense tabletop
lab.intro: Create a synthetic document pack with three benign policy documents and three documents containing clearly labeled adversarial instructions. Use a mock agent workflow on paper or in a local sandbox. The goal is to verify controls, not to discover a live model exploit. Record whether the agent's goal changes, whether it proposes an unauthorized tool call, and whether the enforcement layer blocks it.
tasks: Label each source by provenance, owner, trust level and permitted use.
Write expected behavior for direct and indirect injection attempts.
Define the tool policy independently of prompt wording.
Test whether the workflow preserves the original user objective over multiple turns.
Specify a safe fallback when intent is ambiguous or the requested operation is consequential.
lab.evidence: A source-trust table, ten tabletop cases, expected-versus-observed results and remediation notes.
lab.model: The policy documents are allowed to provide facts about cancellation terms; their embedded instructions are not authorized to alter application policy. A robust design tags retrieved passages with source metadata, limits retrieval to the relevant corpus, keeps credentials out of model-visible context, and routes tool calls through an authorization service. The mock agent can produce a draft answer but cannot send passport data. A test passes only if no prohibited side effect occurs—not merely if the model says it refused. Include a delayed multi-turn test to detect goal drift and persistent memory contamination.

rubric.competent: Independent, scoped, testable enforcement

rubric.competent: Clear artifacts, negative tests and traceable results

quiz.q: What is the central security problem in indirect prompt injection?
o: Untrusted content is allowed to influence behavior as if it had instruction authority.
quiz.why: The core issue is authority confusion between application instructions and data being processed.

quiz.q: Why are delimiters alone insufficient?
o: They do not create a deterministic security boundary for model behavior.
quiz.why: Formatting can aid interpretation but cannot enforce permissions or guarantee model behavior.

quiz.q: What should a prompt-injection test measure?
o: Only whether the model says ‘I refuse’.
Whether unauthorized state changes or disclosures occur, including across multiple steps.
Whether the attack text is grammatically correct.
quiz.why: Security outcomes are about actual behavior and side effects, not just generated refusal language.

lessons.title: Tool, API and MCP Security
lessons.lead: Secure the capability layer through which agents interact with enterprise systems.

slides.title: Tools are executable authority
slides.html:
Tools are executable authority

Learning objective — Explain and apply: tools are executable authority.

Core principle

A tool is not merely a function description; it is an interface to data, computation or side effects under some identity.

Applied scenario

A 'lookup customer' tool can expose regulated records if resource-level authorization is absent.

Engineering response

Inventory capabilities and effective privileges from implementation and backend behavior.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

What determines a tool's true power: its name, schema or backend authority?

slides.title: Design narrow tool contracts
slides.html:
Design narrow tool contracts

Learning objective — Explain and apply: design narrow tool contracts.

Core principle

Small, purpose-specific tools reduce ambiguity and make authorization, validation and audit easier.

Applied scenario

Replace a generic SQL tool with customer-scoped read and separately governed update operations.

Engineering response

Prefer typed inputs, explicit targets, bounded results and no arbitrary command parameters.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Why is a generic execute-anything tool difficult to secure?

slides.title: API authorization at the resource
slides.html:
API authorization at the resource

Learning objective — Explain and apply: api authorization at the resource.

Core principle

Authorization must check the requested object and operation at the backend, not rely on agent-level access alone.

Applied scenario

A support agent may read only cases assigned to the requesting customer's tenant.

Engineering response

Enforce tenant, owner, role, purpose and field-level restrictions on every call.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Where should object-level authorization be performed?

slides.title: Schema and parameter validation
slides.html:
Schema and parameter validation

Learning objective — Explain and apply: schema and parameter validation.

Core principle

Typed schemas constrain structure but must also validate semantics, ranges, ownership and business invariants.

Applied scenario

A valid invoice ID can still be paired with an invalid payee account or excessive amount.

Engineering response

Reject unknown fields, unsafe defaults, oversized inputs and ambiguous identifiers.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

What is the difference between syntactic schema validation and semantic authorization?

slides.title: MCP architecture and trust boundaries
slides.html:
MCP architecture and trust boundaries

Learning objective — Explain and apply: mcp architecture and trust boundaries.

Core principle

MCP standardizes host-client-server interaction, but protocol compatibility does not guarantee secure deployment.

Applied scenario

A host connects to a third-party MCP server that exposes filesystem and browser tools.

Engineering response

Model host, client, server, transport, tool metadata, resources and credential boundaries separately.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Which MCP component should not be treated as inherently trusted merely because it speaks the protocol?

slides.title: MCP server onboarding
slides.html:
MCP server onboarding

Learning objective — Explain and apply: mcp server onboarding.

Core principle

Server onboarding should assess provenance, publisher, code, dependencies, permissions, transport and operational owner.

Applied scenario

An employee adds an unreviewed server that requests access to internal documents.

Engineering response

Use approved registries, allowlists, code review, signed artifacts and controlled rollout.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

What minimum evidence should be required before an MCP server enters production?

slides.title: Tool descriptions and poisoning
slides.html:
Tool descriptions and poisoning

Learning objective — Explain and apply: tool descriptions and poisoning.

Core principle

Tool metadata can mislead model selection or expand apparent capability; descriptions are not security policy.

Applied scenario

A tool description falsely claims it is read-only while the implementation can modify records.

Engineering response

Compare advertised behavior with tested implementation and enforce a server-side capability contract.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

How should the client behave when tool metadata conflicts with observed permissions?

slides.title: Transport, sessions and replay
slides.html:
Transport, sessions and replay

Learning objective — Explain and apply: transport, sessions and replay.

Core principle

Authenticated transport, session binding, request integrity and replay controls protect tool interactions.

Applied scenario

A captured approval-bearing request is replayed after the original user has left the session.

Engineering response

Bind requests to principal, audience, nonce, expiry and task context; use TLS and robust session handling.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Which fields help prevent an old tool request being replayed in a new context?

slides.title: MCP credentials and secrets
slides.html:
MCP credentials and secrets

Learning objective — Explain and apply: mcp credentials and secrets.

Core principle

Long-lived shared credentials create broad blast radius and obscure which agent initiated an action.

Applied scenario

Several agents share one API key, making revocation and attribution difficult after compromise.

Engineering response

Use per-agent or per-task short-lived credentials, secret brokers and automatic rotation.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Why should tool servers avoid receiving a user's master credential?

slides.title: Tool output filtering and chaining
slides.html:
Tool output filtering and chaining

Learning objective — Explain and apply: tool output filtering and chaining.

Core principle

Outputs may contain malicious instructions, secrets or oversized content that affects later model calls.

Applied scenario

A compromised tool returns a payload that redirects a downstream agent to a second tool.

Engineering response

Validate output types, size, provenance and policy; inspect every hop in a tool chain.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

What must happen before a tool response enters another agent's context?

slides.title: Side effects, idempotency and transactions
slides.html:
Side effects, idempotency and transactions

Learning objective — Explain and apply: side effects, idempotency and transactions.

Core principle

Agent retries and partial failures can create duplicate, inconsistent or irreversible changes.

Applied scenario

A timeout after a payment request leads the agent to submit the payment again.

Engineering response

Use idempotency keys, transaction states, reconciliation and compensating actions.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

How does idempotency protect against uncertain execution outcomes?

slides.title: MCP security verification lab
slides.html:
MCP security verification lab

Learning objective — Explain and apply: mcp security verification lab.

Core principle

A secure MCP review tests declared capability, actual behavior, identity, isolation, data exposure and auditability.

Applied scenario

Compare a server's advertised read-only tool with an instrumented test that attempts a write in a sandbox.

Engineering response

Document findings with reproducible requests, expected policy result and remediation owner.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

What test would reveal a server that silently exceeds its declared tool scope?

guide: Model Context Protocol and similar tool interfaces standardize how hosts discover and invoke capabilities. They do not make a connected server trustworthy, and protocol conformance is not a security certification. A tool's name, description, input schema, output schema, annotations and version can all affect model selection or client behavior. Treat tool metadata as part of the attack surface: review it, pin approved definitions, detect changes and require reapproval when capabilities or semantics change. A tool that appears read-only can still expose sensitive data or trigger indirect side effects through an upstream system.

For remote MCP servers, implement the current protocol's authorization model and follow its security considerations. In the 2026-07-28 specification, authorization uses OAuth-based resource protection; servers validate that tokens are intended for that resource, clients use resource indicators, and the specification prohibits token passthrough to upstream APIs. Validate issuer, audience/resource, expiry, signature or introspection result, scopes and tenant. Do not treat a session identifier or opaque state handle as proof of identity. Use HTTPS, validate host/origin as appropriate, protect redirect flows and use PKCE for public clients. SDK behavior can lag the specification, so test the deployed implementation rather than assuming a normative requirement is automatically enforced.

MCP server tools should be isolated like privileged application services. Apply per-tool authorization, strict input schemas, output validation, timeouts, quotas, egress restrictions, secret redaction and central audit. Avoid broad host filesystem or shell access. If the server calls an upstream API, obtain a separate upstream credential with the minimum scope; never forward the caller's bearer token. Human confirmation should be bound to the exact action and parameters for high-impact operations. Monitor tool inventory drift, unexpected server origins, schema changes, unusual call sequences and cross-server shadowing.
lessons.case: An MCP server exposes `search_customer`, `update_customer` and `export_customers`. A developer grants one broad token to the whole server and assumes the tool description ‘read only’ is enough to prevent writes. A malicious or compromised tool definition changes its annotation and description. The client still presents the same approval UI. The secure response is to pin the full tool definition, use per-tool scopes and enforce write authorization inside the server and downstream API.

lab.title: Review an MCP server's trust and authorization posture
lab.intro: Conduct a paper-based review of a fictional MCP service. No server or credentials are required. Use the current 2026-07-28 protocol security requirements as the versioned reference, and explicitly note where a real deployment must verify SDK support.
tasks: Inventory server origin, transport, tools, schemas, annotations, owners and versions.
Define resource-specific OAuth token validation: issuer, audience, expiry, scope and signature/introspection.
Show why a caller token cannot be forwarded to an upstream API.
Define schema pinning, change approval, per-tool authorization and output validation.
Write negative tests for wrong audience, expired token, missing scope, unapproved origin and changed tool schema.
lab.evidence: MCP security review checklist, token-validation matrix, tool inventory and five negative test cases.
lab.model: The server accepts only a token issued for its own resource, validates issuer, audience, lifetime and scope on every protected request, and rejects invalid or under-scoped requests. It obtains its own narrowly scoped token for any upstream service. Tool definitions are versioned and cryptographically pinned as an integrity measure; a changed schema triggers review, not silent acceptance. The server independently checks authorization for each tool, validates parameters, constrains filesystem/network access, and logs the action without secrets. The course should not imply optional message-level signing is a universal protocol requirement; distinguish mandatory specification controls from additional defense-in-depth patterns.
