quiz.q: What does MCP standardization provide?
o: A common protocol surface; implementations still need authentication, authorization and isolation.
A guarantee that tool descriptions are safe.
A guarantee that prompts cannot be injected.
quiz.why: The protocol enables interoperability; security depends on specification requirements and implementation controls.

quiz.q: Why must an MCP server validate token audience/resource?
o: To ensure the token was issued for this resource and not another service.
quiz.why: A valid token for another API must not be accepted by the MCP server.

quiz.q: What should happen when a tool schema changes after approval?
o: Ignore the change if the name is unchanged.
Detect drift and require review/reapproval before use.
quiz.why: Tool metadata can change capability and client behavior; integrity monitoring is required.

lessons.title: Agentic Identity and Access Management
lessons.lead: Give agents accountable identities and task-scoped authority across delegated workflows.

slides.title: Agents as non-human identities
slides.html:
Agents as non-human identities

Learning objective — Explain and apply: agents as non-human identities.

Core principle

An agent instance needs a distinct, attributable identity rather than an informal shared service account.

Applied scenario

A finance agent and a customer-service agent must not appear as the same principal in audit records.

Engineering response

Register owner, purpose, environment, lifecycle, credential source and permitted capabilities.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Why is a single shared agent identity inadequate for incident attribution?

slides.title: Human identity versus agent identity
slides.html:
Human identity versus agent identity

Learning objective — Explain and apply: human identity versus agent identity.

Core principle

The user who initiates a task, the agent that executes it and the service that performs the action are distinct principals.

Applied scenario

An employee asks an agent to retrieve a contract; the backend must still enforce the employee's document rights.

Engineering response

Preserve the initiating subject and the executing workload identity through every authorization decision.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Which identities should appear in the audit event for a delegated action?

slides.title: Workload identity foundations
slides.html:
Workload identity foundations

Learning objective — Explain and apply: workload identity foundations.

Core principle

Workload identity provides cryptographically verifiable identity for running software without relying on static shared secrets.

Applied scenario

A containerized agent obtains a short-lived identity assertion from a trusted workload platform.

Engineering response

Adopt mature workload identity patterns such as SPIFFE/SPIRE where they fit the environment.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

What problem does workload identity solve that an environment variable API key does not?

slides.title: OAuth and delegated authorization
slides.html:
OAuth and delegated authorization

Learning objective — Explain and apply: oauth and delegated authorization.

Core principle

OAuth scopes and token exchange can carry delegated authority, but must be constrained to the intended task and audience.

Applied scenario

A calendar agent receives permission to create one event, not broad mailbox access.

Engineering response

Use narrow scopes, audience restriction, consent, expiry and resource-server enforcement.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Why should a token's audience be restricted to the intended service?

slides.title: Task-scoped and ephemeral credentials
slides.html:
Task-scoped and ephemeral credentials

Learning objective — Explain and apply: task-scoped and ephemeral credentials.

Core principle

Credentials should expire with the task and carry only the authority required for the next action.

Applied scenario

A temporary export token expires after the approved report is generated.

Engineering response

Issue just-in-time credentials and revoke them when task state or risk changes.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

What is the security benefit of a task-bound token over a week-long bearer token?

slides.title: Delegation chains and authority attenuation
slides.html:
Delegation chains and authority attenuation

Learning objective — Explain and apply: delegation chains and authority attenuation.

Core principle

Each delegation should preserve provenance while narrowing—not silently expanding—the authority passed downstream.

Applied scenario

A coordinator delegates read-only research to a sub-agent without passing its own write credential.

Engineering response

Represent parent task, delegated scope, expiry, constraints and revocation relationship.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

What does authority attenuation mean in a multi-hop agent chain?

slides.title: Confused deputy prevention
slides.html:
Confused deputy prevention

Learning objective — Explain and apply: confused deputy prevention.

Core principle

A confused deputy uses its own stronger authority to perform an action the requester could not perform.

Applied scenario

A report agent retrieves restricted employee records because its service account has global access.

Engineering response

Authorize the user-agent-action-resource tuple at the data service and avoid ambient authority.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

How does per-resource authorization prevent the classic confused-deputy pattern?

slides.title: Policy decision and enforcement points
slides.html:
Policy decision and enforcement points

Learning objective — Explain and apply: policy decision and enforcement points.

Core principle

A policy decision point evaluates context; a policy enforcement point blocks or permits the actual operation.

Applied scenario

A policy engine checks user role, data sensitivity, amount and task purpose before a payment API call.

Engineering response

Keep policy evaluation separate from the model and fail closed for high-impact actions.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Why should the model not be the final policy enforcement point?

slides.title: Dynamic authorization context
slides.html:
Dynamic authorization context

Learning objective — Explain and apply: dynamic authorization context.

Core principle

Authorization may depend on risk, time, device, location, data sensitivity, transaction amount and current task state.

Applied scenario

A low-value refund is allowed automatically, while an unusual high-value refund requires approval.

Engineering response

Use context-aware policies with explainable deny reasons and bounded exceptions.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Which context signals should never independently grant privilege?

slides.title: Privileged agent access
slides.html:
Privileged agent access

Learning objective — Explain and apply: privileged agent access.

Core principle

Administrative and high-impact tools require just-in-time access, strong separation of duties and session monitoring.

Applied scenario

A cloud remediation agent can propose a firewall change but cannot approve and deploy its own change.

Engineering response

Separate plan, approve and execute roles; record all privileged sessions and outputs.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

How can separation of duties prevent an autonomous agent from self-authorizing?

slides.title: Identity lifecycle and revocation
slides.html:
Identity lifecycle and revocation

Learning objective — Explain and apply: identity lifecycle and revocation.

Core principle

Agents need joiner-mover-leaver controls for creation, ownership changes, suspension, rotation and retirement.

Applied scenario

A retired pilot agent's token remains valid after its owner leaves the organization.

Engineering response

Automate credential expiry, orphan detection, ownership recertification and kill-switch revocation.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

What should happen to delegated credentials when an agent is suspended?

slides.title: Agent identity architecture exercise
slides.html:
Agent identity architecture exercise

Learning objective — Explain and apply: agent identity architecture exercise.

Core principle

A complete design binds agent identity, task identity, human initiator, delegated scope and final resource authorization.

Applied scenario

Trace a user-approved invoice query through coordinator, extraction agent, finance API and audit log.

Engineering response

Produce an identity sequence diagram and test both allowed and denied delegation paths.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Can the organization prove who initiated, which agent acted and under what authority?

guide: Agent identity must be explicit, unique, attributable and governed across the agent lifecycle. A workload identity answers which software component is acting; a human identity answers on whose behalf and under which delegated authority; a tool identity identifies the service receiving the request. These are related but not interchangeable. Avoid a single shared service account for an entire agent fleet. Separate identities by environment, agent role, tenant and capability where practical, and make the authority chain visible in logs and policy decisions.

Authorization should be evaluated at action time against the actual resource and current business context. Combine role or attribute-based policy with resource ownership, purpose, transaction attributes, data classification and separation-of-duties rules. A delegation grant should be explicit, bounded by action, resource, amount or volume, tenant, purpose, expiry and revocation. It should not permit the agent to create a more privileged sub-agent or silently widen scope. For delegated workflows, preserve the chain of custody: initiating principal, agent workload, delegated grant, downstream service and final actor. A model's natural-language assertion about who authorized an action is not an identity assertion.

Use short-lived, audience-bound credentials from an identity provider or workload identity system; store secrets in a managed vault and avoid exposing them in prompts, traces or tool results. Refresh and revoke grants deliberately. Test confused-deputy conditions: can a privileged server be induced to use its own broad credential on behalf of an unprivileged caller? Can a token for service A be replayed at service B? Can a background task continue after the user's grant expires? Can a sub-agent exceed the parent's authority? These are authorization tests, not prompt-quality tests.
lessons.case: A finance analyst asks an agent to prepare a supplier payment batch. The agent has a service identity with payment-write access. A malicious supplier record asks the agent to change the bank account and execute immediately. The system cannot prove whether the analyst authorized the changed destination. The correct design uses the analyst's verified identity for policy context, a constrained agent workload identity, an independent payment policy and a second approver for beneficiary changes.

lab.title: Design delegated identity and least-privilege grants
lab.intro: Create a role and delegation model for the finance workflow. Use fictional identities and payment records. Define grants as structured policy data rather than natural-language instructions.
tasks: Define identities for requester, agent workload, payment tool, approver and downstream payment service.
Write a delegation grant with subject, actor, audience, actions, resources, limits, purpose, expiry and revocation handle.
Create allow and deny rules for beneficiary changes, payment amounts and cross-tenant access.
Model sub-agent delegation and prove authority cannot expand down the chain.
Specify token storage, rotation, revocation and audit requirements.
lab.evidence: Identity map, sample grant schema, policy table, revocation sequence and audit event example.
lab.model: The initiating analyst remains the accountable human principal; the agent has a distinct workload identity; the payment service validates a token specifically intended for it. A grant allows preparation but not final execution, and it excludes beneficiary modification. Any changed beneficiary requires a separate verified approval workflow. A child agent receives no more authority than its parent grant and has its own identity. Expired or revoked grants stop queued work at execution time. Logs preserve actor, subject, delegated scope, policy version and approval event while never storing bearer tokens.

rubric.competent: Independent, scoped, testable enforcement

quiz.q: Why is one shared service account for all agents dangerous?
o: It obscures attribution and encourages excessive shared privilege.
quiz.why: Shared credentials collapse boundaries and make least privilege and accountability difficult.

quiz.q: Which fields should a delegated grant include?
o: Action, resource, audience, limits, purpose, expiry and revocation context.
quiz.why: Delegation must be explicit, bounded and enforceable at the resource boundary.

quiz.q: What is a confused deputy?
o: A model that returns an incorrect answer.
A privileged intermediary misuses its authority on behalf of a less-privileged caller.
A user who forgets a password.
A server that rejects all tokens.
quiz.why: The deputy has authority the requester lacks and is tricked into applying it improperly.

lessons.title: Memory, RAG and Data Security
lessons.lead: Protect information as it is ingested, retained, retrieved, transformed and reused.

slides.title: Data classification for agent workflows
slides.html:
Data classification for agent workflows

Learning objective — Explain and apply: data classification for agent workflows.

Core principle

Classify data by sensitivity, ownership, jurisdiction, purpose and permitted processing before exposing it to agents.

Applied scenario

A support transcript may contain authentication secrets even when its label says 'customer service'.

Engineering response

Apply classification at source and propagate labels through derived records and embeddings.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Why must classification follow data into summaries and vector stores?

slides.title: Memory is a security boundary
slides.html:
Memory is a security boundary

Learning objective — Explain and apply: memory is a security boundary.

Core principle

Memory changes future behavior and should be governed like a database that can influence privileged decisions.

Applied scenario

A stored preference can redirect future reports to an attacker-controlled address.

Engineering response

Define memory schemas, write permissions, provenance, review, expiry and deletion controls.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Which memory write should require explicit validation before persistence?

slides.title: Memory poisoning lifecycle
slides.html:
Memory poisoning lifecycle

Learning objective — Explain and apply: memory poisoning lifecycle.

Core principle

A poisoning path includes attacker-controlled input, memory write, retrieval, interpretation and downstream action.

Applied scenario

An email plants a dormant instruction that is retrieved during a later sensitive workflow.

Engineering response

Test multi-session persistence and quarantine suspicious memory updates.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Why must testing include later sessions rather than only the planting session?

slides.title: Provenance-aware memory
slides.html:
Provenance-aware memory

Learning objective — Explain and apply: provenance-aware memory.

Core principle

Each memory item should retain source, author, timestamp, confidence, trust class and transformation history.

Applied scenario

A fact from an external webpage should not be presented as a verified internal policy.

Engineering response

Store provenance as structured metadata and surface it at retrieval time.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

What information is lost when memory stores only a compressed sentence?

slides.title: RAG ingestion security
slides.html:
RAG ingestion security

Learning objective — Explain and apply: rag ingestion security.

Core principle

Ingestion pipelines must validate source, tenant, file type, content, metadata and update authority.

Applied scenario

A malicious PDF uploaded to a shared knowledge base contaminates retrieval for multiple departments.

Engineering response

Scan, normalize, classify and quarantine content before indexing.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

At which stage should untrusted files be isolated from production retrieval?

slides.title: Vector store isolation
slides.html:
Vector store isolation

Learning objective — Explain and apply: vector store isolation.

Core principle

Embeddings can reveal semantic relationships and must respect tenant boundaries, access controls and deletion requirements.

Applied scenario

A shared vector index returns a neighboring customer's document due to missing metadata filters.

Engineering response

Enforce access control before and after retrieval, and test cross-tenant leakage explicitly.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Why is filtering only after the model sees retrieved chunks too late?

slides.title: Retrieval authorization
slides.html:
Retrieval authorization

Learning objective — Explain and apply: retrieval authorization.

Core principle

The user and agent must be authorized for the source record at retrieval time, not merely at index creation.

Applied scenario

An employee loses access to a project, but old embeddings remain retrievable by an agent.

Engineering response

Re-check source permissions and propagate revocation to indexes and caches.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

What stale-access condition arises when source permissions change after indexing?

slides.title: Data minimization and context budgets
slides.html:
Data minimization and context budgets

Learning objective — Explain and apply: data minimization and context budgets.

Core principle

Only data needed for the task should enter model context; context size is not a justification for broad collection.

Applied scenario

A scheduling agent does not need complete HR records to find an employee's availability.

Engineering response

Use field-level projection, redaction, purpose filters and short retention.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

How does data minimization reduce both privacy and prompt-injection risk?

slides.title: Secrets in prompts, traces and memory
slides.html:
Secrets in prompts, traces and memory

Learning objective — Explain and apply: secrets in prompts, traces and memory.

Core principle

Credentials can leak through prompts, tool results, logs, summaries, crash dumps and observability pipelines.

Applied scenario

A debugging trace captures an API token returned by a misconfigured tool.

Engineering response

Use secret detection, tokenization, redaction and strict access controls across telemetry and memory.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Which secondary data stores should be included in a secret-leak review?

slides.title: Retention, deletion and correction
slides.html:
Retention, deletion and correction

Learning objective — Explain and apply: retention, deletion and correction.

Core principle

Agent systems must support retention limits, legal holds, deletion propagation and correction of derived knowledge.

Applied scenario

A deleted customer record remains in a vector index and a cached agent summary.

Engineering response

Map data lineage and implement deletion workflows for source, cache, embedding and backup layers.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

How can an organization verify that deletion propagated to derived stores?

slides.title: Privacy and cross-border processing
slides.html:
Privacy and cross-border processing

Learning objective — Explain and apply: privacy and cross-border processing.

Core principle

Agent workflows may send prompts and retrieved data to model providers, tool vendors and regions with different legal regimes.

Applied scenario

A regional healthcare agent routes patient notes to a model endpoint in another jurisdiction.

Engineering response

Maintain data-flow maps, processor controls, transfer assessments and region-aware routing.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Which external recipients must be included in a privacy impact assessment?

slides.title: Memory and RAG assurance exercise
slides.html:
Memory and RAG assurance exercise

Learning objective — Explain and apply: memory and rag assurance exercise.

Core principle

Assurance requires tests for poisoning, leakage, stale permissions, provenance loss and deletion failures.

Applied scenario

Seed a synthetic poisoned note, retrieve it later, then verify the policy engine blocks the resulting sensitive action.

Engineering response

Record retrieval traces, source IDs, access decisions and residual exposure.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

What evidence demonstrates that memory controls work across sessions?

guide: RAG and memory extend the data-security boundary beyond the prompt. The system may ingest files, email, web pages, tickets, databases, vector embeddings, summaries, caches and persistent notes. Security must follow the data through ingestion, indexing, retrieval, model context, tool use, logs, backups and deletion. A document can be authorized for storage but not for every user's retrieval. Enforce access at retrieval time using the requesting principal and current entitlements; do not rely only on permissions copied into a vector index at ingestion.

Preserve provenance and metadata such as source, owner, tenant, classification, purpose, timestamp, retention, consent and integrity status. Chunking and embedding must not strip the controls needed downstream. Retrieval should enforce tenant and document-level authorization before content reaches the model. Treat retrieved content as untrusted data even when the source is authenticated. Prevent cross-tenant nearest-neighbor leakage, unauthorized citation, cache bleed and prompt injection through indexed content. Use encryption and access controls for source stores, vector databases, embedding services, caches and logs.

Memory is particularly sensitive because it can persist attacker-controlled content and influence future actions. Define what may be remembered, who can write it, how it is validated, when it expires and how users can correct or delete it. Separate factual memory from instructions and policy. Record provenance and confidence; do not allow retrieved memory to silently override current system policy or the authenticated user's request. Deletion must cover derived artifacts where applicable: source documents, chunks, embeddings, caches, summaries, replicas and backups according to documented retention and legal requirements.
lessons.case: A legal assistant indexes matter files from several clients. A shared vector index returns a highly similar chunk from the wrong matter. The chunk includes privileged advice and an injected instruction. The agent cites it in a draft for another client. The failure is a retrieval authorization defect compounded by provenance loss; prompt filtering alone cannot repair the underlying cross-matter access violation.

lab.title: Design a secure RAG and memory lifecycle
lab.intro: Use a synthetic dataset with three tenants, public policy documents and confidential case files. Design the ingest, index, retrieve, cite, remember, correct and delete paths. Do not upload real personal or confidential data.
tasks: Define metadata required on every chunk and memory record.
Write retrieval authorization rules for tenant, matter, user, purpose and classification.
Specify how provenance survives chunking, embedding, reranking and summarization.
Create a memory poisoning test and a cross-tenant retrieval test.
Write a deletion workflow covering derived artifacts, caches and documented backup retention.
lab.evidence: Data-flow map, metadata schema, retrieval policy, test cases and deletion runbook.
lab.model: Authorization is applied before content is sent to the model and rechecked when the underlying entitlement changes. Each chunk carries tenant, matter, source ID, owner, classification, retention and provenance. The model can cite only authorized chunks. Memory writes are limited to an allowlisted schema and cannot store instructions that supersede system policy. Poisoned content is quarantined and traceable to source. Deletion propagates through source, index, embeddings, caches and summaries; backups follow a documented expiry process, and the organization records what cannot be immediately purged. The course should distinguish logical deletion from verified physical erasure.

quiz.q: Where should RAG authorization be enforced?
o: Only when the source document is first uploaded.
At retrieval time using current identity, tenant and resource permissions.
Only by asking the model to respect access labels.
quiz.why: Ingestion-time permissions can become stale; authorization must be checked when data is retrieved.

quiz.q: Why preserve provenance through chunking and embeddings?
o: To support authorization, attribution, correction, retention and deletion.
To remove the need for encryption.
quiz.why: Provenance and metadata enable governance and traceability across derived representations.

quiz.q: What is a memory poisoning risk?
o: Attacker-controlled content persists and influences later agent behavior.
A model forgets a harmless preference.
quiz.why: Persistent memory can carry hostile instructions or false facts across sessions and contexts.

lessons.title: Multi-Agent Security and Trust Propagation
lessons.lead: Secure delegation, messaging, shared state and emergent behavior in agent networks.

slides.title: Why introduce multiple agents?
slides.html:
Why introduce multiple agents?

Learning objective — Explain and apply: why introduce multiple agents?.

Core principle

Multi-agent decomposition can improve specialization and parallelism but expands identities, interfaces and failure paths.

Applied scenario

A planner delegates research, analysis and execution to separate agents.

Engineering response

Justify each agent boundary with a security and reliability benefit, not novelty alone.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

When does adding another agent increase risk more than capability?

slides.title: Agent roles and capability separation
slides.html:
Agent roles and capability separation

Learning objective — Explain and apply: agent roles and capability separation.

Core principle

Distinct roles should have distinct tools, data scopes and responsibilities to limit collusion and privilege accumulation.

Applied scenario

A research agent reads public sources while an execution agent can update internal records.

Engineering response

Avoid giving every agent the union of all workflow permissions.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

How does role separation constrain a compromised research agent?

slides.title: Authenticated agent messaging
slides.html:
Authenticated agent messaging

Learning objective — Explain and apply: authenticated agent messaging.

Core principle

Messages should identify sender, recipient, task, sequence, integrity and expiry.

Applied scenario

A forged message claiming to come from the compliance agent requests an exception.

Engineering response

Use authenticated channels and signed or otherwise integrity-protected task envelopes.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Which message fields help prevent spoofing and replay?

slides.title: Semantic validation of delegation
slides.html:
Semantic validation of delegation

Learning objective — Explain and apply: semantic validation of delegation.

Core principle

Authenticating a sender does not prove that its requested action is appropriate or within delegated scope.

Applied scenario

A legitimate coordinator asks a read-only analyst to perform an account deletion.

Engineering response

Validate requested capability against the receiver's role and the delegation token.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Why is sender authentication necessary but insufficient?

slides.title: Trust is not transitive
slides.html:
Trust is not transitive

Learning objective — Explain and apply: trust is not transitive.

Core principle

A trusted agent can relay untrusted content; downstream consumers must preserve source provenance rather than inherit trust.

Applied scenario

A trusted summarizer quotes a malicious webpage, which a second agent mistakes for an approved instruction.

Engineering response

Carry trust labels at the data-item level through every handoff.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

What should a receiving agent trust: the sender identity or the provenance of the embedded claim?

slides.title: Shared memory and blackboard risks
slides.html:
Shared memory and blackboard risks

Learning objective — Explain and apply: shared memory and blackboard risks.

Core principle

Shared workspaces can become poisoning, race-condition and cross-agent data-exposure surfaces.

Applied scenario

One agent writes an unverified conclusion that another agent uses to authorize a transaction.

Engineering response

Use write ownership, versioning, provenance, validation and scoped read access.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

How should a shared fact move from proposed to trusted status?

slides.title: Delegation depth and loops
slides.html:
Delegation depth and loops

Learning objective — Explain and apply: delegation depth and loops.

Core principle

Recursive delegation can create unbounded authority chains, runaway cost and hard-to-reconstruct responsibility.

Applied scenario

A sub-agent spawns another agent that creates additional workers with inherited permissions.

Engineering response

Set maximum depth, task budgets, expiry, lineage and explicit re-delegation rules.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Which controls prevent an agent from silently expanding its delegation tree?

slides.title: Collusion and coordinated behavior
slides.html:
Collusion and coordinated behavior

Learning objective — Explain and apply: collusion and coordinated behavior.

Core principle

Agents may reinforce shared errors or coordinate actions that no individual agent appears to own.

Applied scenario

Two agents split a prohibited export into smaller actions to evade a per-call threshold.

Engineering response

Detect cumulative behavior across principals and correlate actions by parent task.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Why must policy evaluate aggregate task effects rather than isolated tool calls?

slides.title: Cascading failure containment
slides.html:
Cascading failure containment

Learning objective — Explain and apply: cascading failure containment.

Core principle

Faults propagate through dependency graphs when downstream systems consume unverified outputs or retry automatically.

Applied scenario

A wrong inventory signal triggers replenishment, finance approval and supplier notification.

Engineering response

Use circuit breakers, confidence thresholds, independent verification and compensating transactions.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Where would you put a circuit breaker in a multi-agent workflow?

slides.title: Human accountability across chains
slides.html:
Human accountability across chains

Learning objective — Explain and apply: human accountability across chains.

Core principle

Delegation must preserve an accountable human or business principal without implying the human approved every downstream action.

Applied scenario

A manager initiates a report; the system must not treat that as approval to email it externally.

Engineering response

Bind human approvals to explicit action scope and record every delegation hop.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

What does a user's initial request authorize—and what does it not authorize?

slides.title: Multi-agent evaluation
slides.html:
Multi-agent evaluation

Learning objective — Explain and apply: multi-agent evaluation.

Core principle

Evaluate end-to-end trajectories, cross-agent messages, shared state, delegated scopes and cumulative impact.

Applied scenario

A test checks whether a malicious tool response can move from research agent to finance agent and cause a payment.

Engineering response

Use adversarial scenarios that span multiple turns and multiple agents.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Why are isolated unit tests inadequate for agent networks?

slides.title: Multi-agent trust architecture exercise
slides.html:
Multi-agent trust architecture exercise

Learning objective — Explain and apply: multi-agent trust architecture exercise.

Core principle

A secure design specifies trust contracts, message schemas, capability boundaries, provenance and revocation for each edge.

Applied scenario

Design a coordinator-researcher-approver-executor chain with separate read, approve and write roles.

Engineering response

Deliver a delegation graph with denied paths and evidence requirements.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Can a compromised upstream agent cause a downstream side effect without an independent authorization check?

guide: Multi-agent architectures multiply trust transitions. Agents may have different roles, tools, model versions, memory stores and owners. A planner may delegate research to a specialist; a specialist may call a tool; the result may be summarized by another agent and passed to an executor. Each handoff can lose provenance, distort constraints or launder authority. A downstream agent must not treat an upstream agent's confidence, role label or natural-language claim as proof that the result is trusted or authorized.

Define contracts between agents: purpose, allowed inputs, output schema, provenance, identity, authority, data classification, expiry and error semantics. Prefer typed, validated messages over free-form instructions for security-relevant fields. Each agent should have its own identity and minimal capabilities. Delegation should be explicit and non-amplifying: a child agent cannot exceed the parent grant. A central policy service can enforce shared rules, but it should not become a single unprotected superuser path. Protect orchestration metadata and task queues against tampering and replay.

Test emergent behavior, not only each agent in isolation. Include collusion-like scenarios, conflicting objectives, cyclic delegation, retry storms, untrusted-agent outputs, role confusion and partial compromise. Measure whether the system preserves constraints over long workflows, not merely whether a final answer looks correct. Ensure a human can identify which agent proposed, approved and executed each operation. A kill switch must stop the whole workflow and revoke outstanding grants, not just terminate the visible front-end agent.
lessons.case: A research agent returns a supplier risk score with a recommendation. A procurement agent interprets the recommendation as authorization to create an order. A finance agent receives the order and schedules payment. None of the handoffs includes evidence of the source, confidence limits or approval state. The system has transformed analysis into execution through a chain of implicit trust.

lab.title: Specify secure inter-agent contracts and delegation
lab.intro: Design a three-agent workflow: researcher, procurement planner and order executor. Keep it fictional. Define what each agent may know, decide and do; then test how a malicious or compromised upstream result is handled.
tasks: Create a role/capability matrix for all three agents.
Define a typed handoff schema with provenance, confidence, source IDs and authorization status.
Prove delegated authority is non-amplifying and bound to the original purpose.
Design tests for conflicting outputs, replay, cyclic delegation and poisoned upstream content.
Specify global cancellation, grant revocation and end-to-end audit correlation.
lab.evidence: Agent interaction diagram, contract schema, delegation table and five multi-agent test cases.
lab.model: The researcher can produce evidence and a recommendation but cannot authorize a purchase. The planner can prepare an order but cannot commit it. The executor requires a separate policy decision and verified approval. The handoff contains structured evidence references and provenance; it does not carry authority merely because the sender is trusted. Each agent uses a distinct identity. Parent grants constrain child grants, and a global cancellation revokes queued work. Test cases verify that a forged `approved=true` field from the researcher is rejected unless backed by a verifiable approval event.

quiz.q: What is authority laundering in a multi-agent system?
o: A downstream agent mistakes an upstream claim or output for authorization.
quiz.why: Authority must be verified, not inherited from a natural-language statement or role label.

quiz.q: What does non-amplifying delegation mean?
o: Each child agent gets admin access.
A child agent cannot receive more authority than the grant of its parent.
quiz.why: Delegation must narrow or preserve the authorized scope, never expand it.

quiz.q: Why test long workflows?
o: Constraints and trust can drift across handoffs, retries and persistent state.
It eliminates the need for unit tests.
quiz.why: Agentic failures can emerge only after multiple interactions and state transitions.

lessons.title: Code Execution, Sandboxing and Isolation
lessons.lead: Contain generated code and tool execution even when model behavior is compromised.

slides.title: Generated code is untrusted code
slides.html:
Generated code is untrusted code

Learning objective — Explain and apply: generated code is untrusted code.

Core principle

Code authored or selected by an agent must be treated like code from an unknown contributor until reviewed and constrained.

Applied scenario

A coding agent runs a generated migration against a production database.

Engineering response

Separate generation, review, test and deployment identities and environments.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

What makes generated code untrusted even when it was produced by an approved model?

slides.title: Execution threat model
slides.html:
Execution threat model

Learning objective — Explain and apply: execution threat model.

Core principle

Execution risk includes command injection, path traversal, dependency abuse, data theft, persistence and lateral movement.

Applied scenario

A build script reads a mounted cloud credential and sends it to an external endpoint.

Engineering response

Model filesystem, process, network, kernel and secret boundaries explicitly.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Which host resources should a code sandbox not inherit by default?

slides.title: Sandbox design principles
slides.html:
Sandbox design principles

Learning objective — Explain and apply: sandbox design principles.

Core principle

A sandbox limits resources, privileges, filesystem visibility, network reachability and lifetime.

Applied scenario

A disposable container runs a generated data-cleaning script with synthetic input and no host mounts.

Engineering response

Use defense in depth: namespaces, seccomp, mandatory access control, resource limits and ephemeral state.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Why is a container alone not a complete security boundary?

slides.title: MicroVMs and stronger isolation
slides.html:
MicroVMs and stronger isolation

Learning objective — Explain and apply: microvms and stronger isolation.

Core principle

MicroVMs can reduce shared-kernel exposure for higher-risk workloads, at added cost and operational complexity.

Applied scenario

An agent executing third-party code is placed in a short-lived microVM with a minimal image.

Engineering response

Match isolation strength to threat model and validate the hypervisor and orchestration plane.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

When might a microVM be justified over a conventional container?

slides.title: Filesystem and workspace controls
slides.html:
Filesystem and workspace controls

Learning objective — Explain and apply: filesystem and workspace controls.

Core principle

Writable paths, mounts, symlinks and temporary directories can expose secrets or enable persistence.

Applied scenario

A build agent modifies a repository's CI configuration to capture later credentials.

Engineering response

Mount only task-specific files, use read-only inputs and discard workspaces after execution.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

How can a persistent workspace turn a one-time compromise into a recurring one?

slides.title: Network egress and metadata protection
slides.html:
Network egress and metadata protection

Learning objective — Explain and apply: network egress and metadata protection.

Core principle

Unrestricted egress enables exfiltration, command-and-control and cloud metadata credential theft.

Applied scenario

A malicious script queries a cloud metadata endpoint from an agent runtime.

Engineering response

Deny by default, proxy approved destinations and block metadata endpoints unless explicitly required.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

What should a sandbox do when a task unexpectedly attempts outbound DNS or HTTP?

slides.title: Secrets and environment inheritance
slides.html:
Secrets and environment inheritance

Learning objective — Explain and apply: secrets and environment inheritance.

Core principle

Environment variables, mounted files, agent context and process arguments can expose credentials to generated code.

Applied scenario

A test runner inherits a production database password from the parent process.

Engineering response

Use secret brokers, scoped ephemeral credentials and clean execution environments.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Why is stripping environment variables a useful but incomplete safeguard?

slides.title: Package and dependency execution
slides.html:
Package and dependency execution

Learning objective — Explain and apply: package and dependency execution.

Core principle

Package managers and build systems execute install hooks and resolve mutable dependency graphs.

Applied scenario

A seemingly ordinary package update runs a post-install script that reads local files.

Engineering response

Pin hashes, use trusted mirrors, inspect lifecycle scripts and build from controlled artifacts.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Why does dependency pinning need integrity verification as well?

slides.title: Resource exhaustion and runaway loops
slides.html:
Resource exhaustion and runaway loops

Learning objective — Explain and apply: resource exhaustion and runaway loops.

Core principle

Agents can create denial of service through recursive plans, huge outputs, repeated API calls or expensive code.

Applied scenario

A retry loop creates thousands of cloud resources after a transient error.

Engineering response

Set budgets for time, tokens, CPU, memory, API calls, spend and delegation depth.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Which budgets should be enforced outside the agent's own reasoning?

slides.title: Browser and desktop automation isolation
slides.html:
Browser and desktop automation isolation

Learning objective — Explain and apply: browser and desktop automation isolation.

Core principle

Browser profiles and desktop sessions may expose cookies, downloads, local files and authenticated internal applications.

Applied scenario

A web agent uses an employee's persistent browser profile and inherits privileged sessions.

Engineering response

Use dedicated ephemeral profiles, domain allowlists, download scanning and action confirmation.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Why should an agent not reuse a human administrator's everyday browser session?

slides.title: Safe code execution pipeline
slides.html:
Safe code execution pipeline

Learning objective — Explain and apply: safe code execution pipeline.

Core principle

A secure pipeline separates proposal, static analysis, sandboxed tests, review, signed artifact and controlled deployment.

Applied scenario

Generated infrastructure code is tested in an isolated account before a human approves promotion.

Engineering response

Make promotion explicit and preserve artifact provenance across stages.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Which stage should be allowed to access production credentials?

slides.title: Isolation validation exercise
slides.html:
Isolation validation exercise

Learning objective — Explain and apply: isolation validation exercise.

Core principle

Isolation must be tested by attempting prohibited access and verifying observable denial, not inferred from configuration.

Applied scenario

Run synthetic probes for host files, metadata endpoints, lateral network access and persistence.

Engineering response

Capture policy, runtime telemetry and evidence that the sandbox terminated cleanly.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

What is the difference between a sandbox configuration review and an isolation test?

guide: Code execution is a high-consequence capability because a model-generated command, script or code artifact can affect files, networks, credentials and production state. Never equate a model's confidence or a tool's declared purpose with safe execution. Treat generated code as untrusted input and isolate it from the host, secrets, control plane and unrelated workloads. The correct isolation design depends on the threat model: process restrictions may be insufficient against hostile code; containers share a kernel; virtual machines provide a stronger boundary but still need hardened configuration; microVMs or dedicated sandboxes can reduce blast radius at additional cost and latency.

Use layered controls: non-root identity, read-only base filesystem, ephemeral workspace, syscall restrictions, resource quotas, CPU/memory/time limits, no host mounts, no Docker socket, no ambient cloud credentials, network egress deny-by-default, explicit dependency sources and destruction after execution. If network access is required, use a controlled proxy with destination allowlists and content inspection. Separate build and runtime identities. Prevent secrets from entering the execution environment unless specifically required and short-lived. Validate artifact type, size and provenance before execution or release.

Define what the sandbox must guarantee and what it does not. A sandbox is not a substitute for application authorization or data classification. Test escape resistance, resource exhaustion, file boundary enforcement, network policy, secret exposure, process persistence and cleanup. For high-consequence operations, prefer structured APIs with constrained parameters over arbitrary shell or code execution. Where code execution is unavoidable, use staged promotion, human review, reproducible builds and signed artifacts.
lessons.case: A developer agent is asked to inspect a repository and run its tests. A test script attempts to read environment variables and connect to an external host. The intended task is local analysis, but the execution environment has the developer's cloud credentials and unrestricted egress. The core issue is ambient authority and an inadequate isolation boundary.

lab.title: Write a sandbox security profile and test plan
lab.intro: Do not execute hostile code. Design a sandbox profile for an agent that must run untrusted test suites against synthetic code. State the minimum capabilities and the controls that prevent access to host secrets and production systems.
tasks: Specify filesystem, process, identity, network, resource and lifetime constraints.
List prohibited mounts and credentials, including host sockets and cloud metadata access.
Define controlled dependency retrieval and outbound network policy.
Write tests for file escape, network egress, resource exhaustion and cleanup.
Identify residual risks and cases where arbitrary code execution should be disabled entirely.
lab.evidence: Sandbox profile, threat assumptions, negative-test matrix and operational teardown checklist.
lab.model: A suitable profile uses an ephemeral non-root environment, read-only base image, isolated writable scratch directory, no host or control-plane mounts, no ambient credentials, deny-by-default egress, controlled package proxy, CPU/memory/process/time quotas and automatic destruction. The execution identity is separate from the agent orchestrator. The sandbox cannot approve production actions; it returns artifacts for separate validation. The design records kernel/runtime assumptions and requires patching and monitoring. If the task can be completed through a structured read-only API, that is safer than running arbitrary code.

quiz.q: Which configuration most reduces sandbox blast radius?
o: Ephemeral non-root execution, no ambient secrets and deny-by-default egress.
A prompt telling the model to behave.
quiz.why: Isolation must remove authority and constrain resources at the operating-system and network layers.

quiz.q: Why are containers not automatically a complete security boundary?
o: They share the host kernel and depend on runtime configuration and hardening.
They replace virtual machines in every threat model.
quiz.why: Containers are useful isolation but do not eliminate kernel, configuration or runtime escape risk.

quiz.q: When should arbitrary code execution be avoided?
o: Whenever a constrained structured API can achieve the same task with materially less authority.
Only when model output is long.
quiz.why: Prefer the narrowest capability that meets the business requirement.

lessons.title: AI Supply Chain and Model Security
lessons.lead: Manage provenance and compromise risk across models, tools, prompts, data and deployment artifacts.

slides.title: The expanded AI supply chain
slides.html:
The expanded AI supply chain

Learning objective — Explain and apply: the expanded ai supply chain.

Core principle

Agentic supply chains include model weights, hosted APIs, orchestration frameworks, tools, skills, prompts, data and evaluators.

Applied scenario

A trusted orchestration package downloads an unreviewed tool extension at runtime.

Engineering response

Maintain a component inventory with owner, source, version, integrity and reachable authority.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Which components should appear in an AI software bill of materials?

slides.title: Model provenance and integrity
slides.html:
Model provenance and integrity

Learning objective — Explain and apply: model provenance and integrity.

Core principle

Model identity, version, source, fine-tuning lineage and serving configuration affect behavior and risk.

Applied scenario

An unapproved model alias silently points production traffic to a different model release.

Engineering response

Pin model identifiers where possible and verify provider change controls and deployment attestations.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Why is a mutable model alias a supply-chain risk?

slides.title: Hosted model provider risk
slides.html:
Hosted model provider risk

Learning objective — Explain and apply: hosted model provider risk.

Core principle

External inference providers may process sensitive prompts, retain logs or change service behavior under contract.

Applied scenario

A legal agent sends confidential contracts to a provider without an approved data-processing arrangement.

Engineering response

Assess data handling, retention, region, access, incident notice, subcontractors and model-change policy.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

What contractual evidence is needed before sensitive data is sent to a model provider?

slides.title: Open-weight model governance
slides.html:
Open-weight model governance

Learning objective — Explain and apply: open-weight model governance.

Core principle

Self-hosting improves control over deployment but transfers responsibility for patching, serving, access and model integrity.

Applied scenario

A downloaded checkpoint is deployed without verifying origin or scanning its packaging format.

Engineering response

Verify hashes and provenance, isolate loading, scan artifacts and harden the inference runtime.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Does local hosting automatically make a model trustworthy? Why not?

slides.title: Fine-tuning and adapter risks
slides.html:
Fine-tuning and adapter risks

Learning objective — Explain and apply: fine-tuning and adapter risks.

Core principle

Fine-tuning datasets and adapters can introduce backdoors, biased behavior or memorized sensitive information.

Applied scenario

A poisoned training example causes a model to recommend a malicious domain under a trigger phrase.

Engineering response

Govern dataset lineage, access, evaluation, release approvals and rollback for adapters.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

What should a model release gate test beyond task accuracy?

slides.title: Prompt, skill and agent-template integrity
slides.html:
Prompt, skill and agent-template integrity

Learning objective — Explain and apply: prompt, skill and agent-template integrity.

Core principle

Prompts and skills are executable behavioral configuration and can alter tool selection or data handling.

Applied scenario

A shared agent skill is updated to instruct the agent to upload local files for debugging.

Engineering response

Version, sign, review and test behavioral artifacts like code.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Why should prompt changes be included in change management?

slides.title: Tool registry and extension security
slides.html:
Tool registry and extension security

Learning objective — Explain and apply: tool registry and extension security.

Core principle

Dynamic tool discovery increases exposure to typosquatting, malicious publishers and permission drift.

Applied scenario

A similarly named tool is installed with broader filesystem permissions than the approved package.

Engineering response

Use trusted registries, publisher verification, package pinning and approval workflows.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

What prevents a malicious update from inheriting the trust of a previously approved tool?

slides.title: Dataset and retrieval corpus provenance
slides.html:
Dataset and retrieval corpus provenance

Learning objective — Explain and apply: dataset and retrieval corpus provenance.

Core principle

Training and retrieval corpora can contain poisoned, stale, unlawful or sensitive material.

Applied scenario

A public dataset includes manipulated policy documents that are later used as enterprise reference content.

Engineering response

Track source lineage, licensing, integrity, quality and removal procedures.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

How is provenance different for training data and live retrieval data?

slides.title: Build and release pipeline protection
slides.html:
Build and release pipeline protection

Learning objective — Explain and apply: build and release pipeline protection.

Core principle

CI/CD for agents must protect secrets, artifacts, tests, policies and deployment approvals.

Applied scenario

A compromised build runner inserts a modified MCP server into the signed release bundle.

Engineering response

Use isolated runners, protected branches, artifact signing, provenance attestations and environment separation.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Which trust assumptions remain if the signing key is stored on the build runner?

slides.title: Vulnerability management for agent components
slides.html:
Vulnerability management for agent components

Learning objective — Explain and apply: vulnerability management for agent components.

Core principle

Traditional CVE scanning must be complemented by behavioral testing of tool permissions and agent workflows.

Applied scenario

A dependency has no known CVE but its update introduces a new network-access capability.

Engineering response

Track both software vulnerabilities and capability changes across versions.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Why is a clean CVE scan not a complete agent security assessment?

slides.title: Vendor and third-party assurance
slides.html:
Vendor and third-party assurance

Learning objective — Explain and apply: vendor and third-party assurance.

Core principle

Vendor assurance should examine architecture, identity, data handling, logging, incident response and change transparency.

Applied scenario

A SaaS agent vendor cannot explain whether delegated tokens are stored or reused across tenants.

Engineering response

Require evidence, test rights, notification terms, exit plans and subprocessor visibility.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Which question reveals whether vendor controls are operational rather than marketing claims?

slides.title: Supply-chain assurance exercise
slides.html:
Supply-chain assurance exercise

Learning objective — Explain and apply: supply-chain assurance exercise.

Core principle

A defensible supply-chain review maps components to owners, provenance evidence, permissions, test results and rollback plans.

Applied scenario

Review a synthetic agent stack with a model API, MCP server, vector database and custom skill package.

Engineering response

Produce a risk-ranked bill of materials and release gate checklist.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Can each component be traced to a verified source and a responsible owner?

guide: The AI supply chain includes model providers, model weights, fine-tuning data, adapters, prompts, orchestration frameworks, SDKs, tools, MCP servers, plugins, containers, dependencies, datasets, evaluation suites and deployment infrastructure. A model identifier alone is not enough to establish what is running. Record provider, model/version, deployment configuration, system prompts, safety settings, adapters, quantization, dependencies, tool inventory and provenance. Changes to any of these may alter behavior or introduce a new attack surface.

Apply software supply-chain discipline: inventory components, pin versions and digests, verify signatures where available, scan dependencies, review licenses and provenance, isolate build pipelines, protect signing keys and maintain a bill of materials appropriate to AI systems. An AI bill of materials should connect models, datasets, fine-tunes, tools, prompts and runtime dependencies to owners and deployment environments. Treat model updates as controlled changes requiring regression testing, not as harmless content refreshes. Vendor assurances are inputs to due diligence, not substitutes for your own controls.

Model-specific risks include poisoned training or fine-tuning data, malicious or vulnerable model artifacts, unsafe serialization, compromised inference endpoints, exposed weights, backdoor behavior, memorization and extraction. Evaluate model behavior against the intended use and threat model. Protect inference endpoints with authentication, quotas and tenant isolation; protect weights and adapters as sensitive intellectual property; monitor model/provider changes; and maintain a rollback path. Distinguish model security from application security: a safer model cannot compensate for an over-privileged tool API.
lessons.case: An organization updates an orchestration SDK and a model version to address performance issues. The SDK silently changes tool-call parsing behavior, while the model update increases the frequency of a particular tool selection. No security regression suite is run. The release creates a new authorization bypass path through an integration that trusted the old parsing behavior.

lab.title: Create an AI supply-chain inventory and release gate
lab.intro: Build a component register for a fictional agent application. Include model, provider, prompts, adapters, SDKs, tools, MCP servers, datasets, containers and external services. Define how a model or tool update is approved and rolled back.
tasks: Create an AI-BOM with version, digest/provenance, owner, environment and criticality.
Identify build and deployment trust boundaries and signing-key controls.
Define model/tool change tests for permissions, prompt injection, output schema and task utility.
Specify vendor due diligence and evidence required for third-party components.
Write a release/rollback decision rule with accountable approvers.
lab.evidence: AI-BOM, supplier assurance checklist, release gate and rollback runbook.
lab.model: The inventory records exact model and SDK versions, tool schemas, prompt/config hashes, data lineage and deployment digest. CI verifies approved artifacts and scans dependencies; release approval includes security regression tests in realistic tool environments. A model update is evaluated for both security and utility because overly restrictive behavior can break workflows and overly permissive behavior can create new risk. Rollback uses a known-good immutable deployment and preserves forensic evidence. No supplier questionnaire alone is sufficient for critical components.

rubric.competent: Clear artifacts, negative tests and traceable results

quiz.q: Why record prompts and tool schemas in an AI-BOM?
o: They influence system behavior and capability exposure and must be versioned and reviewed.
quiz.why: Configuration and capability metadata can materially change agent behavior and authority.

quiz.q: What is a sound model-update practice?
o: Pin the current artifact, test behavior and permissions, then promote with rollback available.
quiz.why: Controlled change management and regression evaluation are essential.

quiz.q: Does a secure model make an over-privileged tool safe?
o: No; application authorization and least privilege remain necessary.
Only if the prompt is long.
Only if the tool is named safely.
quiz.why: Model behavior cannot replace deterministic enforcement at the resource boundary.

lessons.title: Cloud, Network and Infrastructure Security
lessons.lead: Secure the runtime platform and infrastructure that agent workloads depend on.

slides.title: Agent deployment topologies
slides.html:
Agent deployment topologies

Learning objective — Explain and apply: agent deployment topologies.

Core principle

Agents may run in SaaS platforms, private clouds, Kubernetes, serverless functions, desktops or hybrid environments.

Applied scenario

A background agent runs in Kubernetes while its tools execute in separate cloud accounts.

Engineering response

Document control-plane and data-plane paths, tenancy and trust assumptions for each topology.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Which topology decisions change the threat model most significantly?

slides.title: Cloud IAM and agent workloads
slides.html:
Cloud IAM and agent workloads

Learning objective — Explain and apply: cloud iam and agent workloads.

Core principle

Cloud roles attached to agent workloads can expose storage, secrets, queues and administrative APIs.

Applied scenario

A summarization pod inherits a node role that can read unrelated object-storage buckets.

Engineering response

Use workload identity, narrow roles, permission boundaries and resource-level policies.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Why should agent pods not inherit broad node credentials?

slides.title: Kubernetes isolation
slides.html:
Kubernetes isolation

Learning objective — Explain and apply: kubernetes isolation.

Core principle

Namespaces alone do not guarantee isolation; service accounts, network policies, secrets and host access matter.

Applied scenario

An agent pod with privileged mode can escape intended container restrictions.

Engineering response

Apply pod security standards, restricted service accounts, network policies and runtime detection.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Which Kubernetes settings can accidentally grant host-level authority?

slides.title: Network segmentation for agent tools
slides.html:
Network segmentation for agent tools

Learning objective — Explain and apply: network segmentation for agent tools.

Core principle

Segment model inference, tool services, data stores, administration and external egress according to trust.

Applied scenario

A browsing agent should not have a direct route to the production database subnet.

Engineering response

Use explicit service-to-service policies and deny unneeded east-west traffic.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

How does segmentation limit an agent compromised through a public webpage?

slides.title: API gateways and policy proxies
slides.html:
API gateways and policy proxies

Learning objective — Explain and apply: api gateways and policy proxies.

Core principle

Gateways can centralize authentication, quotas, schema validation, logging and policy enforcement for agent API calls.

Applied scenario

All payment calls pass through a gateway that checks transaction limits and task-bound identity.

Engineering response

Ensure gateways validate semantic authorization and cannot be bypassed through alternate paths.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

What risk remains if a gateway checks only token validity?

slides.title: Secrets management infrastructure
slides.html:
Secrets management infrastructure

Learning objective — Explain and apply: secrets management infrastructure.

Core principle

Secret stores should issue short-lived credentials and record which workload requested each secret.

Applied scenario

An agent receives a one-time database credential for a bounded report query.

Engineering response

Avoid static secrets in images, environment files and prompt context; rotate and revoke automatically.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

What telemetry should accompany a secret retrieval event?

slides.title: Storage, queues and event buses
slides.html:
Storage, queues and event buses

Learning objective — Explain and apply: storage, queues and event buses.

Core principle

Asynchronous infrastructure can preserve stale authority and carry attacker-controlled payloads across trust zones.

Applied scenario

A queue message created by a compromised agent is later consumed by a privileged worker.

Engineering response

Authenticate producers, validate schemas, bind messages to task identity and reauthorize at consumption.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Why should a queue consumer not blindly trust an authenticated producer?

slides.title: Data residency and network egress
slides.html:
Data residency and network egress

Learning objective — Explain and apply: data residency and network egress.

Core principle

Model calls and tool requests may move data across regions and organizational boundaries.

Applied scenario

A document-processing agent sends a confidential attachment to an unapproved external endpoint.

Engineering response

Use egress controls, destination allowlists, data-loss prevention and regional routing.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

How can network controls complement prompt-level data protection?

slides.title: Availability and resilience
slides.html:
Availability and resilience

Learning objective — Explain and apply: availability and resilience.

Core principle

Agent workloads can amplify outages through retries, fan-out, recursive delegation and provider dependencies.

Applied scenario

A model timeout causes hundreds of workers to retry simultaneously and overload an internal API.

Engineering response

Use backoff, circuit breakers, concurrency limits, queue controls and graceful degradation.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Which retry strategy avoids turning a transient failure into a cascading outage?

slides.title: Backup, restore and clean recovery
slides.html:
Backup, restore and clean recovery

Learning objective — Explain and apply: backup, restore and clean recovery.

Core principle

Recovery must restore data and policy integrity, not simply restart the agent runtime.

Applied scenario

A poisoned knowledge base is restored from a backup that already contains the malicious memory record.

Engineering response

Version policy and memory stores, test clean restore points and preserve forensic evidence.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

What should be validated before reconnecting an agent after restoration?

slides.title: Infrastructure observability
slides.html:
Infrastructure observability

Learning objective — Explain and apply: infrastructure observability.

Core principle

Infrastructure telemetry should connect workload identity, network flow, API call, task ID and external side effect.

Applied scenario

A suspicious egress connection is correlated with the agent task that read a customer export.

Engineering response

Use consistent trace IDs, time synchronization, protected logs and alertable policy decisions.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

What correlation key makes a distributed agent action traceable end to end?

slides.title: Infrastructure hardening exercise
slides.html:
Infrastructure hardening exercise

Learning objective — Explain and apply: infrastructure hardening exercise.

Core principle

A secure deployment baseline specifies identity, network, storage, secrets, runtime, resilience and recovery controls.

Applied scenario

Harden a synthetic agent namespace and verify denied access to unrelated storage and network segments.

Engineering response

Capture configuration evidence and negative test results for audit.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Can you demonstrate isolation with an observed denied request rather than a checklist alone?

guide: Agentic workloads inherit cloud and infrastructure risks and add dynamic, model-directed control flow. Secure the underlying compute, network, identity, storage, secrets, container orchestration, queues, observability and deployment pipeline using established cloud security practices. Then add controls for agent-specific execution: isolate tenants and workloads, constrain egress, protect metadata services, restrict service-to-service identity, rate-limit inference and tool APIs, and prevent an agent from changing its own deployment or security configuration without controlled approval.

Map every path from the agent runtime to internal and external services. Use network segmentation, private endpoints where appropriate, egress gateways, DNS controls, service mesh identity and explicit destination allowlists. Protect cloud metadata endpoints and workload identity tokens from untrusted code. Separate control plane from data plane. The agent should not be able to modify IAM, logging, network policy, secret stores or its own guardrails merely because those APIs are reachable. Use immutable infrastructure patterns and policy-as-code to reduce drift.

Plan for availability and cost attacks: recursive tool loops, high fan-out, large retrieval requests, queue flooding, provider outages and cascading retries. Set budgets and quotas by user, tenant, agent and tool; apply circuit breakers and backpressure; define graceful degradation and fail-closed behavior for sensitive actions. Backups must include the data and configuration needed to restore service, while recovery tests verify integrity and access control after restoration.
lessons.case: A cloud-hosted research agent can access an internal metadata endpoint, object storage and a deployment API. A compromised code-execution tool can retrieve workload credentials and modify the agent's own network policy. The model did not need administrator-level intent; the runtime environment exposed ambient infrastructure authority.

lab.title: Design cloud guardrails for an agent runtime
lab.intro: Produce a cloud architecture review for a fictional agent workload. Do not deploy or probe infrastructure. Assume a containerized runtime, managed identity, vector store, queue and several SaaS APIs.
tasks: Separate control-plane and workload-plane components and identities.
Define egress destinations, metadata-service protections and secret access paths.
Specify tenant isolation, quotas, backpressure, circuit breakers and graceful degradation.
Prevent the agent from modifying IAM, logging or its own security controls.
Write recovery checks for restored data, policies, keys and audit evidence.
lab.evidence: Cloud trust-boundary diagram, network policy matrix, IAM controls and availability/recovery test plan.
lab.model: The runtime receives a workload identity scoped to the specific services it needs; it cannot access cloud metadata credentials or control-plane APIs. Egress is routed through an allowlisted gateway. The code sandbox has no cloud credentials. Secrets are delivered only to the narrow service that requires them. IAM, logging and network controls are administered through a separate control plane with approval and immutable audit. Quotas and circuit breakers bound runaway behavior. Recovery tests verify policy and key integrity, not merely that containers restart.

rubric.competent: Complete boundary, actors, data and side effects

rubric.partial: Controls named but weakly enforced or evidenced
rubric.competent: Independent, scoped, testable enforcement

rubric.competent: Clear artifacts, negative tests and traceable results
