quiz.q: Why separate control plane from agent workload plane?
o: To prevent the agent from changing the controls that constrain it.
To allow all agents admin access.
quiz.why: A constrained workload should not control its own trust boundary.

quiz.q: What is a safe default for agent egress?
o: Deny by default and permit only justified destinations through controlled policy.
Use DNS names as proof of trust.
Allow any URL returned by a tool.
quiz.why: Explicit egress controls reduce exfiltration and pivot opportunities.

quiz.q: What should recovery testing validate?
o: Restored data, policy, identity, keys and audit integrity.
quiz.why: A functioning but insecure restoration is not a successful recovery.

lessons.title: Secure Agentic Architecture and Zero Trust
lessons.lead: Translate security principles into a coherent reference architecture and design decisions.

slides.title: Zero Trust applied to agents
slides.html:
Zero Trust applied to agents

Learning objective — Explain and apply: zero trust applied to agents.

Core principle

Zero Trust means no implicit trust based on network location, model brand, prior approval or agent-to-agent relationship.

Applied scenario

A trusted internal agent must still reauthorize each sensitive CRM operation.

Engineering response

Continuously evaluate identity, device/workload, resource, action and context.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

What assumption does Zero Trust reject when one agent calls another?

slides.title: Control plane versus reasoning plane
slides.html:
Control plane versus reasoning plane

Learning objective — Explain and apply: control plane versus reasoning plane.

Core principle

The reasoning plane proposes plans; the control plane owns identity, policy, approval and execution enforcement.

Applied scenario

A model suggests deleting records, while an independent policy service checks retention and legal-hold status.

Engineering response

Prevent model-generated text from directly changing authorization policy.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Which plane should decide whether a tool call may execute?

slides.title: Policy-as-code for agent actions
slides.html:
Policy-as-code for agent actions

Learning objective — Explain and apply: policy-as-code for agent actions.

Core principle

Policy-as-code makes allowed actions explicit, versioned, testable and reviewable.

Applied scenario

A policy denies external sharing of confidential files unless a named approver authorizes a specific recipient.

Engineering response

Use deterministic rules for hard boundaries and document any risk-scoring inputs.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Why should high-impact authorization not depend solely on an LLM classifier?

slides.title: Action risk tiers
slides.html:
Action risk tiers

Learning objective — Explain and apply: action risk tiers.

Core principle

Action tiers classify operations by consequence, reversibility, scope and uncertainty.

Applied scenario

Read-only search is low risk; bulk deletion and funds transfer are high risk.

Engineering response

Map tiers to identity assurance, approval, transaction caps, logging and recovery controls.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Which factors should move an action into a higher tier?

slides.title: Human approval as a security control
slides.html:
Human approval as a security control

Learning objective — Explain and apply: human approval as a security control.

Core principle

Human approval is useful only when the reviewer sees a specific, understandable and bounded action.

Applied scenario

An approver reviews exact payee, amount, source account and supporting evidence before a transfer.

Engineering response

Avoid generic approvals and ensure the approved action cannot be mutated afterward.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

How can a system bind approval to the exact action being executed?

slides.title: Transaction design and reversibility
slides.html:
Transaction design and reversibility

Learning objective — Explain and apply: transaction design and reversibility.

Core principle

High-impact actions should be staged, validated, committed once and reconciled afterward.

Applied scenario

A bulk CRM update is previewed, sampled and approved before a transaction commits.

Engineering response

Prefer reversible staging and compensating actions where true rollback is impossible.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Why is a compensating transaction not always equivalent to rollback?

slides.title: Secure defaults and fail-safe behavior
slides.html:
Secure defaults and fail-safe behavior

Learning objective — Explain and apply: secure defaults and fail-safe behavior.

Core principle

When identity, policy, provenance or approval cannot be established, consequential actions should fail closed.

Applied scenario

An unavailable policy service blocks a payment rather than silently allowing it.

Engineering response

Define safe degraded modes that preserve essential read-only functionality.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Which operations can safely continue during policy-service outage?

slides.title: Defense in depth across layers
slides.html:
Defense in depth across layers

Learning objective — Explain and apply: defense in depth across layers.

Core principle

No single prompt filter, model safeguard or gateway can cover every path from influence to impact.

Applied scenario

Prompt screening, scoped identity, tool policy and egress controls each interrupt a different attack stage.

Engineering response

Map controls to attack paths and test whether they are genuinely independent.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

What is the danger of relying on several controls that all depend on the same model judgment?

slides.title: Secure architecture patterns
slides.html:
Secure architecture patterns

Learning objective — Explain and apply: secure architecture patterns.

Core principle

Useful patterns include brokered tools, policy gateways, ephemeral workers, provenance envelopes and human approval for high-impact actions.

Applied scenario

A tool broker exposes narrow operations and checks task-bound authority before calling backend services.

Engineering response

Choose patterns based on threat model and operational constraints, not fashion.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Which pattern prevents agents from holding direct backend credentials?

slides.title: Architecture anti-patterns
slides.html:
Architecture anti-patterns

Learning objective — Explain and apply: architecture anti-patterns.

Core principle

Common anti-patterns include god-mode agents, shared tokens, unrestricted shell, trust-by-prompt and unbounded delegation.

Applied scenario

A single general-purpose agent has admin access to email, cloud, HR and finance systems.

Engineering response

Replace broad capability with task-specific agents and independent policy enforcement.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Which anti-pattern creates the largest blast radius in your environment?

slides.title: Architecture decision records
slides.html:
Architecture decision records

Learning objective — Explain and apply: architecture decision records.

Core principle

Security decisions should record context, alternatives, rationale, consequences, assumptions and review triggers.

Applied scenario

An ADR explains why payment execution requires two-person approval and task-bound tokens.

Engineering response

Link each decision to threat scenarios and measurable acceptance criteria.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

What information makes an architecture decision auditable six months later?

slides.title: Reference architecture exercise
slides.html:
Reference architecture exercise

Learning objective — Explain and apply: reference architecture exercise.

Core principle

A defensible design shows identity issuance, orchestration, memory, tool broker, policy engine, sandbox, telemetry and human control.

Applied scenario

Design a secure customer-operations agent with bounded CRM access and controlled refunds.

Engineering response

Deliver a diagram, policy matrix, threat register and test plan as one coherent architecture pack.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Can every external side effect be traced to an identity, policy decision and evidence record?

guide: A secure agentic architecture uses layered, independently enforced controls. Zero trust means continuously evaluating identity, device/workload posture, resource, context and policy rather than assuming that network location or prior approval creates permanent trust. It does not mean adding a proxy and declaring the architecture zero trust. Least agency is a useful design principle: grant the agent the minimum capability needed for the task, for the shortest duration, with the narrowest resource scope and the lowest possible consequence.

Separate the reasoning plane from the control plane. The reasoning plane interprets goals and proposes actions. The control plane manages identities, policy, approvals, quotas, tool inventory, execution authorization and revocation. The data plane performs the actual read or write. Put policy enforcement close to the resource so that a compromised orchestrator cannot bypass all checks. Use explicit trust zones for user input, external content, model context, internal data, tool execution and privileged services. Every transition should have a contract and a security control.

Architecture decisions should be traceable to requirements and trade-offs. For each high-risk action, specify who may request it, who may approve it, what policy is evaluated, what evidence is recorded, how it is reversed and how it is stopped. Do not use human-in-the-loop as a vague slogan: define the approver's identity, the exact information shown, the time window, whether the approval is single-use, and how the approval is cryptographically or transactionally bound to the operation.
lessons.case: A claims-processing agent can read policy, draft a decision and issue payments. The team proposes a single ‘AI safety gateway’ that inspects prompts and tool calls. The gateway is useful, but if the payment API trusts the orchestrator's broad service token, a compromised orchestrator can bypass the gateway. A layered design enforces authorization again at the payment service.

lab.title: Create a secure reference architecture and ADR
lab.intro: Design a reference architecture for the claims workflow. Include reasoning, control and data planes, trust zones, enforcement points, human approval and failure modes. Write one architecture decision record for the most consequential trade-off.
tasks: Draw trust zones and annotate all data and authority transitions.
Place independent enforcement at the resource boundary for high-impact writes.
Define autonomy tiers and approval conditions for draft, update and payment actions.
Write an ADR explaining alternatives, decision, consequences and residual risk.
Identify bypass paths and prove the control plane cannot be modified by the agent.
lab.evidence: Architecture diagram, control mapping, autonomy policy and one complete ADR.
lab.model: The model cannot directly call the payment processor. It emits a typed proposal to an execution service. The policy engine validates identity, scope, claim ownership, payment amount, destination, fraud state and approval evidence. The payment API performs its own authorization and idempotency checks. The safety gateway is one layer, not the only barrier. The ADR explains why a separate execution service adds latency and complexity but materially reduces the consequence of prompt injection or orchestrator compromise.

rubric.partial: Controls named but weakly enforced or evidenced
rubric.competent: Independent, scoped, testable enforcement

rubric.partial: Some tests; limited negative cases
rubric.competent: Clear artifacts, negative tests and traceable results

rubric.partial: Risks identified without owners or rationale
rubric.competent: Prioritized risks, assumptions, owners and defensible decisions

quiz.q: What is the meaning of least agency?
o: Give the agent broad access to reduce friction.
Give only the minimum capability, scope, duration and consequence needed.
Use one identity for every agent.
quiz.why: Least agency adapts least privilege to autonomous capability and side-effect scope.

quiz.q: Where should critical authorization be enforced?
o: At or near the resource that performs the side effect, with independent checks.
quiz.why: Resource-side enforcement reduces bypass risk from compromised upstream components.

quiz.q: What makes human approval meaningful?
o: A verified approver reviews exact transaction details and grants a bounded, time-limited approval.
quiz.why: Approval needs identity, context, scope, binding and lifecycle controls.

lessons.title: Runtime Enforcement and Formal Assurance
lessons.lead: Move from advisory guardrails to enforceable, testable controls at execution time.

slides.title: Why runtime enforcement matters
slides.html:
Why runtime enforcement matters

Learning objective — Explain and apply: why runtime enforcement matters.

Core principle

A model can produce unsafe actions despite prompts, filters or training; enforcement must sit outside model discretion.

Applied scenario

A maliciously influenced agent proposes an unauthorized database export, and the policy gateway blocks it.

Engineering response

Treat model output as a proposal and require independent authorization before side effects.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

What is the decisive difference between a guardrail and an enforcement point?

slides.title: Policy decision point architecture
slides.html:
Policy decision point architecture

Learning objective — Explain and apply: policy decision point architecture.

Core principle

A policy decision point evaluates principal, action, resource, context, delegation and risk against policy.

Applied scenario

A refund policy checks customer ownership, amount threshold, fraud status and approver identity.

Engineering response

Make decisions deterministic, explainable, versioned and testable.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Which attributes belong in a policy decision request?

slides.title: Policy enforcement point placement
slides.html:
Policy enforcement point placement

Learning objective — Explain and apply: policy enforcement point placement.

Core principle

Enforcement should occur as close as practical to the protected resource and side effect.

Applied scenario

The payment service independently validates a scoped transaction token even if an upstream agent gateway approved it.

Engineering response

Use layered enforcement to prevent bypass through alternate paths.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Why is enforcement only in the orchestrator insufficient?

slides.title: Action contracts and invariants
slides.html:
Action contracts and invariants

Learning objective — Explain and apply: action contracts and invariants.

Core principle

Action contracts define permitted operation, arguments, preconditions, postconditions and failure behavior.

Applied scenario

A contract for 'send invoice' requires verified recipient, approved document, size limit and audit event.

Engineering response

Reject actions that cannot prove required preconditions.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

What precondition prevents a valid email tool from sending a confidential file to an arbitrary recipient?

slides.title: Runtime monitors and state machines
slides.html:
Runtime monitors and state machines

Learning objective — Explain and apply: runtime monitors and state machines.

Core principle

State machines constrain workflow transitions and make illegal sequences detectable.

Applied scenario

A payment workflow cannot transition from 'draft' to 'released' without an independent approval state.

Engineering response

Model allowed states, transitions, timeout and recovery explicitly.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

How does a state machine prevent an agent from skipping a required approval step?

slides.title: Formal methods for critical invariants
slides.html:
Formal methods for critical invariants

Learning objective — Explain and apply: formal methods for critical invariants.

Core principle

Formal specification can express safety properties such as no transfer without approval or no cross-tenant read.

Applied scenario

A temporal property asserts that every high-risk commit is preceded by a valid approval for the same transaction.

Engineering response

Use formal methods selectively where consequences justify precision and verification effort.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Write one safety property for a sensitive agent action in plain language.

slides.title: Capability tokens and constrained execution
slides.html:
Capability tokens and constrained execution

Learning objective — Explain and apply: capability tokens and constrained execution.

Core principle

Capability-based security grants narrowly scoped authority to a specific operation or resource.

Applied scenario

A one-time token permits reading one case record but cannot list the whole customer database.

Engineering response

Bind capability tokens to audience, resource, action, expiry, task and constraints.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

What makes a capability token safer than a general bearer credential?

slides.title: Approval binding and time-of-check/time-of-use
slides.html:
Approval binding and time-of-check/time-of-use

Learning objective — Explain and apply: approval binding and time-of-check/time-of-use.

Core principle

An approval can become unsafe if the action changes between review and execution.

Applied scenario

A payment amount is altered after the manager approves the original request.

Engineering response

Cryptographically or transactionally bind approval to immutable action parameters and recheck at commit.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

What must be compared at execution to prevent approval substitution?

slides.title: Rate limits, budgets and cumulative controls
slides.html:
Rate limits, budgets and cumulative controls

Learning objective — Explain and apply: rate limits, budgets and cumulative controls.

Core principle

Per-call limits do not stop distributed or repeated actions that exceed safe aggregate thresholds.

Applied scenario

An agent issues many small refunds that collectively exceed its daily authorization.

Engineering response

Apply per-agent, per-task, per-user and global budgets with anomaly detection.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Why should rate limits aggregate across a parent task and its child agents?

slides.title: Transactional safety and sagas
slides.html:
Transactional safety and sagas

Learning objective — Explain and apply: transactional safety and sagas.

Core principle

Long workflows need explicit commit points, idempotency, compensation and reconciliation across services.

Applied scenario

A travel agent books a flight but fails to reserve a hotel, requiring a safe compensation path.

Engineering response

Design sagas with clear ownership, retry rules and human escalation for ambiguous states.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

What should the system do when it cannot determine whether a side effect committed?

slides.title: Runtime assurance testing
slides.html:
Runtime assurance testing

Learning objective — Explain and apply: runtime assurance testing.

Core principle

Test enforcement with allowed, denied, boundary, replay, stale-token, outage and bypass scenarios.

Applied scenario

A test changes the target resource after approval and verifies that the commit is rejected.

Engineering response

Measure false allow and false deny rates separately and inspect action traces.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Which negative test is most important for a high-impact tool?

slides.title: Enforcement engineering exercise
slides.html:
Enforcement engineering exercise

Learning objective — Explain and apply: enforcement engineering exercise.

Core principle

A runtime control design specifies policy schema, decision service, enforcement point, evidence and fail-safe behavior.

Applied scenario

Implement a synthetic policy for refunds with amount tiers and immutable approval binding.

Engineering response

Produce test cases proving the model cannot override the policy engine.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Can the enforcement layer still deny an action when the model insists it is safe?

guide: Runtime enforcement converts security policy from documentation into a decision that is checked before an operation affects a resource. The policy input should be structured and authenticated: principal, workload identity, delegated grant, action, resource, tenant, data class, purpose, parameters, current state, risk tier, approval evidence and policy version. The decision should be explicit—permit, deny or require step-up—and the enforcement point should fail safely when policy cannot be evaluated for a high-impact action.

Keep policy evaluation deterministic, testable and separate from model-generated reasoning. A policy engine may use attributes and business rules, but it should not rely on a natural-language explanation as evidence. Bind the decision to the action: a permit for a $50 refund to customer A is not a permit for $500 to customer B. Include a nonce or transaction identifier, expiry and idempotency controls. Re-evaluate when material parameters or state change. Use separation of duties for high-impact operations and maintain an emergency revocation path.

Formal methods can strengthen assurance for critical invariants, but do not overclaim. Model checking, state-machine analysis, type systems, contracts and property-based tests can verify specific properties under stated assumptions. They cannot prove that the model will never be manipulated or that the environment matches the model. Useful invariants include: no cross-tenant access; no write without authorized principal; no payment above limit; no expired grant accepted; no child grant exceeds parent; and no approval reused for a different transaction. Runtime monitors enforce observable properties while tests challenge assumptions.
lessons.case: A travel agent can book flights and hotels. A user approves a $900 itinerary. The model later changes the hotel and total to $1,250 after discovering a better option. A naive system reuses the original approval because the task is still ‘book the trip’. Transaction-bound approval requires a new decision because material parameters changed.

lab.title: Specify and test a runtime authorization policy
lab.intro: Write a small policy specification for a mock refund workflow. Use pseudocode or a policy table; no real API calls. Include allow, deny and step-up outcomes, and bind approvals to exact transaction attributes.
tasks: Define the structured authorization request and decision response.
Write at least six invariants, including tenant isolation, amount limits and grant expiry.
Specify how policy failure, stale state and changed parameters are handled.
Create positive, negative, boundary and replay tests.
Explain which properties could be checked with model checking or property-based tests and their assumptions.
lab.evidence: Policy schema, invariants, test matrix and sample decision trace.
lab.model: A policy request includes subject, actor, audience, tenant, action, resource, amount, currency, case ID, purpose, grant ID, approval ID, timestamp and idempotency key. A decision returns permit/deny/step-up, reason code, policy version and expiry. The executor rechecks state and binds the approval to a canonical transaction hash. Any parameter change invalidates approval. If the policy service is unavailable, high-impact writes fail closed; safe read-only operations may use separately defined degraded behavior. Property tests verify boundary values and cross-tenant cases; formal verification is scoped to the state machine and assumptions.

rubric.competent: Complete boundary, actors, data and side effects

rubric.partial: Controls named but weakly enforced or evidenced
rubric.competent: Independent, scoped, testable enforcement

rubric.partial: Some tests; limited negative cases
rubric.competent: Clear artifacts, negative tests and traceable results

rubric.competent: Prioritized risks, assumptions, owners and defensible decisions

quiz.q: Why bind authorization to transaction parameters?
o: To prevent approval for one operation being reused for a materially different operation.
quiz.why: Transaction binding prevents approval substitution and parameter tampering.

quiz.q: What should happen if policy evaluation is unavailable for a high-impact write?
o: Fail closed or require a separately defined safe fallback.
quiz.why: Critical writes should not proceed without an enforceable current authorization decision.

quiz.q: What can formal methods establish?
o: That all future model behavior is safe.
Specific properties under explicit assumptions and a defined system model.
That vendor software has no bugs.
quiz.why: Formal assurance is powerful but scoped to the properties and assumptions actually modelled.

lessons.title: Monitoring, Detection and Digital Forensics
lessons.lead: Make agent behavior observable, attributable and reconstructable without creating new data leaks.

slides.title: Why agent observability differs
slides.html:
Why agent observability differs

Learning objective — Explain and apply: why agent observability differs.

Core principle

Agent traces need to capture task, identity, delegation, tool, policy decision, data provenance and side effect—not just prompts and tokens.

Applied scenario

A SOC analyst needs to know which retrieved document preceded a privileged API call.

Engineering response

Define a minimum event schema before deploying agents to production.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Which event fields make an agent action reconstructable?

slides.title: End-to-end task correlation
slides.html:
End-to-end task correlation

Learning objective — Explain and apply: end-to-end task correlation.

Core principle

A stable task identifier links model calls, tool invocations, child agents, queue messages and external transactions.

Applied scenario

A parent task ID connects a coordinator's request to a sub-agent's CRM update.

Engineering response

Propagate correlation identifiers across synchronous and asynchronous boundaries.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

How can investigators link a payment event to the initiating human request?

slides.title: Identity and delegation telemetry
slides.html:
Identity and delegation telemetry

Learning objective — Explain and apply: identity and delegation telemetry.

Core principle

Logs should show who initiated, which workload acted, what authority was delegated and which policy version decided.

Applied scenario

An event records user subject, agent workload ID, task token scope and resource decision.

Engineering response

Record delegation lineage without exposing raw secrets.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

What evidence is lost if logs record only the shared service account?

slides.title: Prompt and context telemetry safely
slides.html:
Prompt and context telemetry safely

Learning objective — Explain and apply: prompt and context telemetry safely.

Core principle

Context telemetry can aid investigation but may contain sensitive data and attacker-controlled instructions.

Applied scenario

A trace captures a malicious email excerpt that later influenced tool selection.

Engineering response

Use selective capture, redaction, access controls, retention limits and secure evidence storage.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

How can responders preserve useful context without storing every secret verbatim?

slides.title: Tool-call and side-effect logs
slides.html:
Tool-call and side-effect logs

Learning objective — Explain and apply: tool-call and side-effect logs.

Core principle

Record tool name, version, arguments or safe hashes, target, result, policy decision and transaction identifier.

Applied scenario

A log distinguishes an attempted refund from a committed refund.

Engineering response

Instrument at the tool broker and backend so missing or bypassed events are detectable.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Why should tool invocation and backend commit be logged separately?

slides.title: Behavioral baselines for agents
slides.html:
Behavioral baselines for agents

Learning objective — Explain and apply: behavioral baselines for agents.

Core principle

Baseline task duration, tool sequence, data volume, delegation depth and action frequency by agent role.

Applied scenario

A research agent suddenly begins exporting thousands of customer records.

Engineering response

Detect deviations using context-aware thresholds and avoid treating every unusual sequence as malicious.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Which baseline signals can reveal privilege misuse even when each call is authorized?

slides.title: Detection engineering for prompt injection
slides.html:
Detection engineering for prompt injection

Learning objective — Explain and apply: detection engineering for prompt injection.

Core principle

Detection can combine provenance, suspicious content, tool-chain anomalies and attempted policy violations.

Applied scenario

A tool output containing hidden instructions is followed by an unexpected request to access secrets.

Engineering response

Correlate content signals with behavior; do not rely on keyword detection alone.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Why should detection prioritize attempted impact over suspicious wording alone?

slides.title: Memory and retrieval forensics
slides.html:
Memory and retrieval forensics

Learning objective — Explain and apply: memory and retrieval forensics.

Core principle

Investigations must identify what was stored, when, by whom, from which source and which later tasks retrieved it.

Applied scenario

A poisoned memory record is linked to three downstream agent sessions.

Engineering response

Version memory stores and retain provenance and retrieval event metadata.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

What chain of evidence links a memory poisoning event to later impact?

slides.title: Tamper-evident audit records
slides.html:
Tamper-evident audit records

Learning objective — Explain and apply: tamper-evident audit records.

Core principle

High-assurance workflows may require signed events, immutable storage, trusted timestamps and verifiable sequence integrity.

Applied scenario

A regulated payment action produces a cryptographically verifiable receipt of policy and approval.

Engineering response

Protect logs from the same agent and administrator paths being monitored.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

What threat does tamper-evident logging address that ordinary application logs do not?

slides.title: Privacy-aware telemetry
slides.html:
Privacy-aware telemetry

Learning objective — Explain and apply: privacy-aware telemetry.

Core principle

Observability can become a secondary repository of confidential prompts, customer data and credentials.

Applied scenario

A verbose debug trace stores entire health records even though the production action needed only a status flag.

Engineering response

Apply data minimization, masking, access review, retention and purpose limitation to telemetry.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Which telemetry fields should be hashed, masked or omitted?

slides.title: SOC workflows and alert triage
slides.html:
SOC workflows and alert triage

Learning objective — Explain and apply: soc workflows and alert triage.

Core principle

Security operations need agent-specific playbooks, severity criteria, kill switches and escalation ownership.

Applied scenario

An alert identifies a finance agent using an unexpected tool after retrieving an untrusted attachment.

Engineering response

Correlate with identity, endpoint, cloud and business-system telemetry before classifying impact.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

What makes an agent alert actionable rather than just a model-anomaly notification?

slides.title: Forensic reconstruction exercise
slides.html:
Forensic reconstruction exercise

Learning objective — Explain and apply: forensic reconstruction exercise.

Core principle

A defensible investigation reconstructs initiating request, context sources, decisions, authority, actions and downstream state.

Applied scenario

Analyze a synthetic timeline in which a document injection causes a denied export attempt and a successful low-value write.

Engineering response

Separate observed facts, inferred reasoning and unknowns in the incident timeline.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Can you state exactly what happened without pretending to know hidden model cognition?

guide: Monitoring agentic systems requires event-level observability across intent, plan, context, policy, tool execution and state change. A conventional application log that records only HTTP status codes is insufficient. Capture a correlation ID, authenticated user, workload identity, delegated grant, model/provider/version, tool and schema version, source provenance, policy decision, approval event, resource, action, outcome, latency and cost. Preserve enough evidence to reconstruct a sequence without indiscriminately logging sensitive prompts, credentials or personal data.

Useful detections include unusual tool combinations, privilege escalation attempts, cross-tenant retrieval, schema drift, repeated denied calls, unexpected egress, abnormal memory writes, high fan-out, runaway loops, excessive spend, unusual time-of-day activity and actions outside an approved workflow. Baselines must account for legitimate variability. Detection should be tied to response playbooks: revoke a grant, disable a tool, isolate a workload, quarantine a memory source, block egress or pause a workflow. Alerting without a tested containment action is incomplete.

Forensics must preserve provenance and chain of custody. Keep clocks synchronized; record immutable or tamper-evident events; retain policy and tool versions; protect log access; and document gaps caused by provider-side black boxes. Do not assume the full hidden reasoning trace is available or necessary. Focus on observable decisions and effects. Redact tokens, secrets and unnecessary personal information. Define retention and access controls for logs because telemetry itself can become a sensitive data store.
lessons.case: An agent issues several unusual data queries followed by a bulk export. The model trace is incomplete because the provider does not expose internal reasoning. The organization can still reconstruct the event from tool calls, identity tokens' non-secret metadata, policy decisions, data access logs, approval records and outbound network telemetry.

lab.title: Build an agentic audit event and detection plan
lab.intro: Design observability for a fictional agent with retrieval, email and refund tools. Work with synthetic event records. Define what must be logged, what must be redacted and which patterns should trigger containment.
tasks: Define a canonical event schema for proposal, policy decision, approval, execution and result.
Create five detections with signal, threshold rationale, false-positive considerations and response.
Write a forensic timeline for a suspected data export.
Define tamper-evidence, retention, access and secret-redaction requirements.
Identify telemetry gaps and compensating evidence sources.
lab.evidence: Event schema, detection catalogue, sample timeline and logging standard.
lab.model: The event model correlates the user request to the exact tool action and resulting resource change. It records identities and decision metadata but excludes bearer tokens and raw secrets. The export detection correlates unusual query volume, sensitive classification, new destination and outbound transfer. Containment revokes the agent grant, disables export, blocks egress and preserves logs. Forensics records source system, time, collector, integrity hash and analyst actions. Missing provider reasoning is documented as a limitation, not filled by speculation.

rubric.competent: Independent, scoped, testable enforcement

rubric.competent: Clear artifacts, negative tests and traceable results

quiz.q: What is the most useful audit design?
o: Store every secret and full prompt forever.
Correlate identity, proposal, policy decision, approval, tool call and outcome while minimizing sensitive content.
quiz.why: Useful observability balances reconstruction, accountability and data minimization.

quiz.q: Why should detections have response playbooks?
o: Detection without a defined containment action may not reduce impact.
quiz.why: A detection should lead to an actionable, tested response.

quiz.q: What if the model provider does not expose hidden reasoning?
o: Invent a likely chain of thought.
Use observable tool, identity, policy and state-change evidence; document the gap.
quiz.why: Forensics should rely on verifiable evidence, not fabricated internal reasoning or secrets.

lessons.title: Agentic Red Teaming and Security Evaluation
lessons.lead: Test real execution paths and measure security, utility and resilience under adversarial conditions.

slides.title: Why ordinary chatbot testing is inadequate
slides.html:
Why ordinary chatbot testing is inadequate

Learning objective — Explain and apply: why ordinary chatbot testing is inadequate.

Core principle

Agent security must be assessed through trajectories and side effects, not only generated answers.

Applied scenario

A model refuses a malicious prompt but still calls a tool that leaks the requested data.

Engineering response

Capture full state transitions, tool calls, approvals and backend outcomes.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

What is the most important test artifact beyond the model's final text?

slides.title: Define evaluation objectives
slides.html:
Define evaluation objectives

Learning objective — Explain and apply: define evaluation objectives.

Core principle

A useful evaluation states threat model, protected property, attacker capability, environment and success criterion.

Applied scenario

Test whether an external attacker can cause a cross-tenant record read through indirect injection.

Engineering response

Pre-register allowed outcomes and impact metrics before running tests.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Why should success criteria be defined before the red-team exercise?

slides.title: Build a safe test environment
slides.html:
Build a safe test environment

Learning objective — Explain and apply: build a safe test environment.

Core principle

Use synthetic data, isolated accounts, resettable environments and explicit authorization for testing.

Applied scenario

A simulated payroll API uses fake employees and cannot reach production banking rails.

Engineering response

Prohibit live credential use and uncontrolled external targets in training labs.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

What prevents a realistic lab from becoming an operational attack?

slides.title: Prompt injection test matrix
slides.html:
Prompt injection test matrix

Learning objective — Explain and apply: prompt injection test matrix.

Core principle

Vary source, modality, language, encoding, placement, context length and attack timing.

Applied scenario

Test an instruction in a webpage, PDF, email, image OCR and tool response.

Engineering response

Use reproducible payload families and document model/runtime versions.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Which dimensions reveal whether a defense generalizes beyond one prompt?

slides.title: Long-horizon and multi-turn attacks
slides.html:
Long-horizon and multi-turn attacks

Learning objective — Explain and apply: long-horizon and multi-turn attacks.

Core principle

Adaptive attacks exploit state accumulation, retries, task transitions and delayed activation.

Applied scenario

A harmless-looking email plants memory that triggers an exfiltration attempt in a later session.

Engineering response

Evaluate multi-session persistence and attacker adaptation, not only one-turn refusal.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Why can a defense pass a single-turn benchmark and fail in production?

slides.title: Tool-chain and privilege escalation tests
slides.html:
Tool-chain and privilege escalation tests

Learning objective — Explain and apply: tool-chain and privilege escalation tests.

Core principle

Test whether low-risk tools can be combined into high-impact outcomes or reach unauthorized resources.

Applied scenario

A search result steers a browser agent into a file tool that can read private workspace data.

Engineering response

Instrument every hop and enforce cumulative policy across the chain.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

What test exposes a tool-chain confused deputy?

slides.title: Identity and delegation tests
slides.html:
Identity and delegation tests

Learning objective — Explain and apply: identity and delegation tests.

Core principle

Test forged principals, stale tokens, replay, scope expansion, cross-tenant access and revocation.

Applied scenario

A child agent attempts to use a parent token after its task has expired.

Engineering response

Verify backend denials and audit evidence for each invalid delegation path.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Which identity failure could remain invisible if you test only prompt responses?

slides.title: Memory poisoning tests
slides.html:
Memory poisoning tests

Learning objective — Explain and apply: memory poisoning tests.

Core principle

Test untrusted writes, dormant payloads, retrieval triggers, deletion and cross-session contamination.

Applied scenario

Plant a synthetic malicious preference and verify it is quarantined or blocked at later retrieval.

Engineering response

Measure persistence, activation conditions and downstream action attempts.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

What does a memory poisoning evaluation need to measure besides initial write success?

slides.title: Sandbox escape and egress tests
slides.html:
Sandbox escape and egress tests

Learning objective — Explain and apply: sandbox escape and egress tests.

Core principle

Probe filesystem boundaries, metadata services, network egress, process privileges and persistence.

Applied scenario

A synthetic script attempts to read a fake host secret and contact a controlled sink.

Engineering response

Use safe canaries and verify that attempted access is denied and logged.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Which result is stronger evidence: a policy document or a denied sandbox probe?

slides.title: Metrics: safety, utility and resilience
slides.html:
Metrics: safety, utility and resilience

Learning objective — Explain and apply: metrics: safety, utility and resilience.

Core principle

Measure attack success, unauthorized side effects, task utility, false blocks, recovery time and reproducibility.

Applied scenario

A detector with high F1 may still miss the rare high-impact path that matters most.

Engineering response

Report confidence intervals, scenario coverage and failure severity; avoid headline accuracy alone.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Why must security evaluation include benign task utility?

slides.title: Benchmark limitations and generalization
slides.html:
Benchmark limitations and generalization

Learning objective — Explain and apply: benchmark limitations and generalization.

Core principle

Benchmarks can be narrow, static, contaminated or mismatched to real architectures and threat models.

Applied scenario

A detector performs well on known payload templates but fails on contextual manipulation.

Engineering response

Use held-out scenarios, adaptive attackers, external environments and independent replication.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

What evidence supports a claim that a defense generalizes?

slides.title: Purple-team remediation cycle
slides.html:
Purple-team remediation cycle

Learning objective — Explain and apply: purple-team remediation cycle.

Core principle

A mature exercise converts findings into owners, architectural fixes, regression tests and retest evidence.

Applied scenario

A red-team finding on shared tokens becomes a remediation project with a negative authorization test.

Engineering response

Track exploit path, root cause, control owner, due date, residual risk and retest result.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

When is a red-team finding actually closed?

guide: Agentic red teaming must test complete tasks and state transitions, not just prompt-response pairs. A useful evaluation includes the model, orchestration framework, tool definitions, identities, memory, retrieval corpus, policy engine, runtime enforcement and downstream resources. Test both security and utility: a system that blocks every action is secure only in a trivial sense and may fail its business purpose. Define the threat model, scope, safety constraints, test data, success criteria and stop conditions before testing.

Use a layered test strategy: component tests for schema and policy; integration tests for identity and tool boundaries; adversarial tests for direct and indirect injection; long-horizon tests for objective drift and memory poisoning; multi-agent tests for trust propagation; and operational tests for logging, revocation and recovery. AgentLAB's 2026 ICML paper is useful evidence that long-horizon attacks—such as intent hijacking, tool chaining, task injection, objective drifting and memory poisoning—deserve dedicated evaluation. Its reported benchmark scale is evidence about that benchmark, not a universal guarantee about production systems.

Measure outcomes at the resource boundary. Examples include unauthorized reads, unauthorized writes, cross-tenant disclosure, approval bypass, tool misuse, policy evasion, persistence of hostile memory, recovery time and task completion under attack. Track false positives and false negatives. Repeat tests after model, prompt, tool, policy, data or infrastructure changes. Keep a reproducible test corpus and version every run. Red-team findings should become engineering tickets with owner, severity, evidence, remediation and retest—not just a slide deck.
lessons.case: A vendor demonstrates that its agent refuses a set of known malicious prompts. Your own application connects the model to internal tools and persistent memory. A long-horizon scenario plants a false instruction in a shared record and triggers it in a later task. The vendor's prompt benchmark does not test your system's state, permissions or side effects.

lab.title: Design a reproducible agent security evaluation
lab.intro: Create a controlled test plan for a mock research-and-refund agent. No external targets, live credentials or real transactions. Include short and long-horizon scenarios, negative controls and utility checks.
tasks: Define scope, assumptions, attacker capabilities and prohibited test actions.
Create test cases for prompt injection, tool chaining, memory poisoning, authorization bypass and resource exhaustion.
Measure actual state changes and disclosures, not only textual responses.
Include utility metrics and benign cases to identify overblocking.
Version the environment and produce a retestable findings report.
lab.evidence: Evaluation plan, test catalogue, metrics, run record and prioritized remediation report.
lab.model: Each test has a unique ID, preconditions, initial state, attack path, expected policy result, observed resource effect, evidence and severity. Long-horizon cases preserve memory and task state across turns. A pass requires that the prohibited side effect does not occur and that the system produces an auditable denial or safe fallback. Benign controls verify that legitimate read and draft tasks still work. Findings are retested against the same environment version and after every relevant change.

quiz.q: What is the primary evaluation target for an agentic system?
o: The end-to-end system and its actual state changes under adversarial tasks.
quiz.why: The security boundary includes tools, identity, memory, policy and downstream effects.

quiz.q: What does AgentLAB contribute?
o: A benchmark for adaptive long-horizon attack susceptibility in agent environments.
quiz.why: AgentLAB motivates testing multi-turn, chained and persistent attacks; it is not a certification.

quiz.q: Why include benign utility tests?
o: To make the system appear secure.
To detect overblocking and measure whether the system still performs its intended task safely.
quiz.why: Security and utility must be evaluated together to avoid trivial deny-all outcomes.

lessons.title: Incident Response, Containment and Recovery
lessons.lead: Prepare to stop, investigate and recover from agent-enabled incidents.

slides.title: Agent incident response lifecycle
slides.html:
Agent incident response lifecycle

Learning objective — Explain and apply: agent incident response lifecycle.

Core principle

Use established incident response phases but add agent identity, memory, delegated tasks, tool access and external side effects.

Applied scenario

A compromised agent requires more than shutting down its model endpoint; its tokens and queued tasks may persist.

Engineering response

Extend playbooks to include orchestration, tool servers, memory stores and downstream systems.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Which agent-specific assets must be contained during response?

slides.title: Detection-to-containment decisions
slides.html:
Detection-to-containment decisions

Learning objective — Explain and apply: detection-to-containment decisions.

Core principle

Containment should stop harmful actions quickly while preserving evidence and business continuity.

Applied scenario

Disable payment tools for one agent while leaving read-only customer support available.

Engineering response

Prepare scoped kill switches for task, agent, credential, tool and environment.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Why is a global shutdown not always the best first response?

slides.title: Revoke credentials and delegated authority
slides.html:
Revoke credentials and delegated authority

Learning objective — Explain and apply: revoke credentials and delegated authority.

Core principle

Compromise response must revoke active and refresh credentials and invalidate child delegations.

Applied scenario

A parent agent is suspended, but its child token remains usable against a data API.

Engineering response

Maintain a delegation graph and test transitive revocation.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

How do you prove no descendant task can continue acting after parent compromise?

slides.title: Stop queues, retries and scheduled tasks
slides.html:
Stop queues, retries and scheduled tasks

Learning objective — Explain and apply: stop queues, retries and scheduled tasks.

Core principle

Background work can continue after the visible agent session ends.

Applied scenario

A queued export job runs minutes after an operator closes the chat session.

Engineering response

Provide task cancellation, queue draining, retry suppression and scheduler inventory.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Which asynchronous execution paths must be checked during containment?

slides.title: Preserve volatile and persistent evidence
slides.html:
Preserve volatile and persistent evidence

Learning objective — Explain and apply: preserve volatile and persistent evidence.

Core principle

Evidence includes runtime state, prompts, retrieved content, tool traces, memory versions, tokens metadata and backend transactions.

Applied scenario

An investigator snapshots a poisoned memory store before quarantining it.

Engineering response

Define evidence capture procedures that preserve chain of custody and minimize sensitive exposure.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

What evidence may disappear if the agent is immediately reset?

slides.title: Determine scope and blast radius
slides.html:
Determine scope and blast radius

Learning objective — Explain and apply: determine scope and blast radius.

Core principle

Scope includes data read, data written, external recipients, child agents, tool versions and affected users.

Applied scenario

A single compromised coordinator may have delegated tasks across several business units.

Engineering response

Use task lineage and backend audit logs to enumerate actual side effects.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Why is reviewing only the parent agent's logs insufficient?

slides.title: Memory and knowledge-base remediation
slides.html:
Memory and knowledge-base remediation

Learning objective — Explain and apply: memory and knowledge-base remediation.

Core principle

Eradication requires finding and removing poisoned content from source documents, memory, indexes, caches and summaries.

Applied scenario

Deleting one vector record does not remove the malicious instruction from its original email attachment.

Engineering response

Track content lineage and validate clean re-indexing after remediation.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

How can the same poison re-enter after a memory store is cleaned?

slides.title: Recover with clean authority
slides.html:
Recover with clean authority

Learning objective — Explain and apply: recover with clean authority.

Core principle

Recovery should reissue credentials, restore verified policy and data, and restart with constrained capabilities.

Applied scenario

A finance agent returns in read-only mode while the team validates transaction history.

Engineering response

Use staged restoration, canary workflows and explicit reauthorization.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

What conditions should be met before restoring write access?

slides.title: Customer, regulator and partner communication
slides.html:
Customer, regulator and partner communication

Learning objective — Explain and apply: customer, regulator and partner communication.

Core principle

Communications must distinguish confirmed exposure, attempted action, actual impact and uncertainty.

Applied scenario

An unauthorized export was blocked, but telemetry shows no evidence of data leaving the environment.

Engineering response

Coordinate legal, privacy, security and business owners before making definitive claims.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Why should a blocked attempt not be described as a confirmed data breach?

slides.title: Root cause and control failure analysis
slides.html:
Root cause and control failure analysis

Learning objective — Explain and apply: root cause and control failure analysis.

Core principle

Look beyond the immediate prompt or model behavior to missing authorization, excessive privilege, weak provenance or inadequate monitoring.

Applied scenario

The root cause is a shared token and missing resource check, not merely that the model followed a malicious email.

Engineering response

Use causal analysis and identify systemic fixes that prevent recurrence.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Which root-cause statement leads to a durable architectural improvement?

slides.title: Post-incident learning and regression
slides.html:
Post-incident learning and regression

Learning objective — Explain and apply: post-incident learning and regression.

Core principle

Convert incidents into threat-model updates, policy changes, test cases, training and vendor requirements.

Applied scenario

A new regression suite verifies that malicious tool outputs cannot trigger privileged actions.

Engineering response

Track recurrence, control effectiveness and residual risk over time.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

What evidence shows that lessons learned changed system behavior?

slides.title: Tabletop exercise
slides.html:
Tabletop exercise

Learning objective — Explain and apply: tabletop exercise.

Core principle

A realistic tabletop tests decision rights, technical kill switches, evidence access and communication under uncertainty.

Applied scenario

Simulate a memory-poisoned agent that attempts an unauthorized supplier payment through a child agent.

Engineering response

Score time to contain, authority revocation, evidence quality and recovery safety.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Can the team stop the action, identify its scope and restore safely within agreed objectives?

guide: Incident response for agentic systems extends conventional preparation, detection, containment, eradication, recovery and lessons learned. The response team must be able to identify every agent instance, workload identity, tool connection, delegated grant, memory store, queue and downstream resource. A single ‘disable agent’ button may stop new requests but leave queued jobs, long-lived tokens, child agents, webhooks or scheduled tasks running. Build a complete inventory and test revocation across the execution graph.

Containment actions should be graduated and evidence-aware: pause a workflow, revoke a specific grant, disable a tool, quarantine a source or memory namespace, block egress, isolate a runtime, rotate credentials or shut down the whole service. Preserve logs and state before destructive cleanup where feasible. Avoid deleting the very memory, queue or configuration needed to understand the incident. For suspected data disclosure, identify data accessed, recipients, copies, retention and legal notification obligations with counsel and the data owner.

Recovery requires more than restarting the model. Rebuild from known-good artifacts, rotate compromised secrets, restore trusted policy and tool definitions, revalidate permissions, review memory and retrieval sources, clear poisoned state where appropriate and run security regression tests before re-enabling autonomy. Establish explicit recovery gates and rollback criteria. Conduct a post-incident review that identifies architectural causes, not only the prompt or model behavior that exposed them.
lessons.case: A compromised tool server begins returning manipulated outputs and triggers abnormal data access. The visible agent process is stopped, but a queued background task and delegated token remain active. The incident continues. Effective containment requires revoking grants, disabling the server, pausing queues and checking downstream systems.

lab.title: Run an agentic incident-response tabletop
lab.intro: Use a fictional incident: suspected prompt injection has led to unauthorized customer-data export. Simulate the response with role cards for incident commander, identity owner, platform operator, data owner, legal/privacy contact and business owner.
tasks: Define severity, initial facts, uncertainty and decision authority.
Identify all active identities, delegated grants, child agents, queues and tools.
Choose containment actions and state what evidence must be preserved first.
Determine data scope, affected tenants, external recipients and notification decision inputs.
Write recovery gates and post-incident corrective actions.
lab.evidence: Incident timeline, containment checklist, impact assessment, recovery plan and lessons-learned record.
lab.model: The commander establishes a timeline and assigns technical workstreams. Identity operations revoke the specific delegated grants and rotate any exposed secrets. Platform operations disable the affected tool server, pause queues and block suspicious egress. Data owners determine what records were accessed and whether copies left controlled systems. Forensics preserves tool outputs, policy decisions, access logs and queue state. Recovery requires clean tool definitions, known-good deployment, reviewed memory, revalidated authorization and a red-team regression test. Legal notification is assessed by jurisdiction and contract; the course does not prescribe one universal deadline.

rubric.partial: Controls named but weakly enforced or evidenced
rubric.competent: Independent, scoped, testable enforcement

rubric.competent: Clear artifacts, negative tests and traceable results

rubric.competent: Prioritized risks, assumptions, owners and defensible decisions

quiz.q: Why is stopping the visible agent process insufficient?
o: Queued jobs, tokens, webhooks and delegated agents may continue operating.
The model will restart itself every time.
quiz.why: Containment must revoke authority and stop all active execution paths.

quiz.q: What should be preserved during containment?
o: Relevant logs, tool outputs, policy decisions and state needed for forensics, subject to privacy controls.
quiz.why: Evidence preservation must be balanced with safe secret handling and privacy.

quiz.q: What is a proper recovery gate?
o: Known-good artifacts, rotated secrets, reviewed memory, revalidated policy and regression tests pass.
A manager says it is fine.
quiz.why: Recovery must restore trusted state and prove security controls work before autonomy resumes.

lessons.title: Governance, Regulation and Enterprise Risk
lessons.lead: Create accountable governance without confusing voluntary guidance with binding law.

slides.title: Governance for agentic systems
slides.html:
Governance for agentic systems

Learning objective — Explain and apply: governance for agentic systems.

Core principle

Governance defines who may deploy agents, for what purposes, under what controls and with what accountability.

Applied scenario

A business unit cannot connect a new agent to HR data without owner, risk review and approved controls.

Engineering response

Establish an agent inventory, risk tiers, approval gates and lifecycle review.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

What governance decision must precede production access to sensitive data?

slides.title: Map existing cybersecurity frameworks
slides.html:
Map existing cybersecurity frameworks

Learning objective — Explain and apply: map existing cybersecurity frameworks.

Core principle

NIST CSF, SP 800-53, ISO 27001 and zero-trust principles remain useful but need agent-specific implementation detail.

Applied scenario

An access-control control is extended to cover tool calls, delegated authority and agent identity.

Engineering response

Map agent controls to existing enterprise control owners to avoid parallel governance silos.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Why should agent security extend rather than replace established cybersecurity governance?

slides.title: NIST AI RMF and agent risks
slides.html:
NIST AI RMF and agent risks

Learning objective — Explain and apply: nist ai rmf and agent risks.

Core principle

AI risk management should connect context, measurement, governance and management to the actual agent lifecycle.

Applied scenario

An agent's risk profile changes when it receives a new write tool or begins retaining memory.

Engineering response

Reassess risk at design, release, material change and retirement.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Which lifecycle changes should trigger a fresh risk assessment?

slides.title: OWASP guidance and its limits
slides.html:
OWASP guidance and its limits

Learning objective — Explain and apply: owasp guidance and its limits.

Core principle

OWASP agentic risks provide a practical threat checklist, but they are not a certification or complete control framework.

Applied scenario

A team maps goal hijack and memory poisoning to system controls and test evidence.

Engineering response

Use OWASP categories to structure analysis, then tailor to assets, architecture and business impact.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

What should a team not claim merely because it completed an OWASP checklist?

slides.title: CISA and international agency guidance
slides.html:
CISA and international agency guidance

Learning objective — Explain and apply: cisa and international agency guidance.

Core principle

Joint government guidance emphasizes constrained autonomy, layered defense, identity, oversight, threat modelling and continuous assessment.

Applied scenario

A critical infrastructure operator pilots an agent in read-only mode before granting operational control.

Engineering response

Use government guidance as a baseline and document where local risk requires stronger controls.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Which recommendations apply even when the agent is supplied as a managed service?

slides.title: Privacy and data protection obligations
slides.html:
Privacy and data protection obligations

Learning objective — Explain and apply: privacy and data protection obligations.

Core principle

Privacy duties attach to personal data processing by agents, including purpose, minimization, security, transparency and rights handling.

Applied scenario

An HR agent summarizes employee records and creates derived profiles that may affect decisions.

Engineering response

Map legal bases, data subjects, processors, transfers, retention and automated decision implications.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Why do summaries and inferred attributes still require privacy governance?

slides.title: Sector and jurisdiction mapping
slides.html:
Sector and jurisdiction mapping

Learning objective — Explain and apply: sector and jurisdiction mapping.

Core principle

Applicable obligations depend on sector, data type, location, use case and whether the system makes regulated decisions.

Applied scenario

A healthcare agent may face different requirements from a marketing-content assistant.

Engineering response

Create a jurisdiction and sector applicability register with counsel and compliance owners.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Why is a single global 'AI compliance' checkbox inadequate?

slides.title: Third-party and outsourcing governance
slides.html:
Third-party and outsourcing governance

Human oversight and meaningful control

Oversight must be proportionate, informed and operationally capable of stopping or reversing actions.

A clinician receives a decision-support summary but retains independent clinical judgment and access to source evidence.

Risk registers and control ownership

A useful register links scenario, impact, likelihood, existing controls, evidence, owner, deadline and residual risk.

Applied scenario

A memory-poisoning risk is assigned to the data platform owner with a retrieval test as acceptance evidence.

Engineering response

Avoid ownerless risks and controls with no measurable effectiveness test.

What is missing from a risk register entry that only says 'add guardrails'?

Assurance cases and audit evidence

Learning objective — Explain and apply: assurance cases and audit evidence.

Core principle

An assurance case connects claims, arguments and evidence that the system is acceptably safe and secure for a defined use.

Applied scenario

The claim 'refund agent cannot exceed $500' is supported by policy tests, backend enforcement and audit samples.

Engineering response

State scope, assumptions, evidence freshness and known limitations explicitly.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

What evidence would substantiate a claim about a maximum transaction amount?

slides.title: Governance operating model
slides.html:
Governance operating model

Learning objective — Explain and apply: governance operating model.

Core principle

A mature operating model integrates security, architecture, legal, privacy, procurement, product and business accountability.

Applied scenario

An AI governance board reviews high-impact agent capabilities while platform teams own technical controls.

Engineering response

Define decision rights, escalation paths, exceptions and periodic recertification.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Who can approve an exception, and who independently verifies its controls?

guide: Governance turns technical controls into an operating model. Every deployed agent needs an accountable business owner, technical operator, data owner, security contact, lifecycle status, purpose, approved use, autonomy tier, risk classification and review cadence. Governance should cover procurement, design, development, testing, deployment, change, monitoring, incident response, retirement and deletion. Shadow agents and personal tokens are governance failures because they bypass inventory, identity and risk review.

Map applicable laws, regulations, contracts and sector rules by jurisdiction and role. Do not assume one global AI law or one generic privacy rule resolves every deployment. Assess whether the organization is provider, deployer, importer, operator or data controller/processor under relevant regimes; identify cross-border data flows, records obligations, consumer rights, human oversight and critical-sector requirements. In the Caribbean context, evaluate local privacy, cybersecurity, financial, public-sector and critical-infrastructure obligations with qualified counsel and regulators. This course teaches a governance method, not jurisdiction-specific legal advice.

Use risk tiers linked to autonomy and impact. Low-impact drafting may need ordinary access controls and review; high-impact decisions or irreversible writes require stronger validation, human approval, monitoring and recovery. Governance evidence should include system cards, architecture diagrams, threat models, data maps, supplier records, evaluation reports, policy tests, approval logs, incidents and change records. Risk acceptance must name an accountable decision-maker, scope, duration, rationale, compensating controls and review date.
lessons.case: A department deploys a meeting assistant using a personal API key and a shared mailbox. It is not listed in the enterprise inventory and retains meeting transcripts indefinitely. When it begins drafting supplier commitments, nobody can identify the business owner or the data retention basis. The immediate task is not to tune the prompt; it is to bring the system under governance or suspend it.

Supplier updates trigger change review. Retirement includes revoking credentials, disabling endpoints, deleting or retaining data according to policy and preserving required records. Risk acceptance is time-bound and cannot waive mandatory legal obligations.

Critical-sector risk is contextual

Financial services and payments

A Caribbean public service deploys a multilingual citizen assistant using a foreign-hosted model and local records.

slides.title: Sector-specific assurance exercise
slides.html:
Sector-specific assurance exercise

Learning objective — Explain and apply: sector-specific assurance exercise.

Core principle

A sector assurance profile translates general controls into hazards, regulatory obligations, evidence and autonomy limits.

Applied scenario

Compare a bank payment agent, hospital documentation agent and energy maintenance agent.

Engineering response

Produce three risk profiles with different approval, isolation and recovery requirements.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Why should one generic autonomy policy not govern all three sectors?

guide: Critical industries require hazard-informed security engineering. A financial agent may initiate transfers; a healthcare agent may influence clinical decisions or expose health records; an energy agent may interact with operational technology; a public-sector agent may affect eligibility or access to services. The same generic autonomy setting is inappropriate because consequence, reversibility, safety requirements, latency, human oversight and regulatory obligations differ. Separate information support from decision authority and operational control.

In healthcare, distinguish administrative assistance from clinical decision support and from direct control of treatment or devices. Require provenance, patient-context controls, clinician oversight, privacy protections and validated downtime procedures. In finance, enforce transaction limits, beneficiary verification, fraud controls, segregation of duties and immutable audit. In energy and industrial environments, keep agentic systems away from safety instrumented functions and real-time control unless a rigorous sector-specific safety case supports a narrowly bounded role; default to read-only advisory use and established OT segmentation. In public services, protect due process, explainability appropriate to the decision, appeal paths, accessibility and non-discrimination review.

For every sector, define safe state, failover, manual override, incident coordination, supplier dependency and recovery. Evaluate concentration risk where critical services depend on a small number of foreign cloud, model or connectivity providers. Regional deployments should plan for cross-border data transfers, service continuity during connectivity outages, local skills and incident response capacity. Avoid treating ‘human in the loop’ as a substitute for engineering controls; a human must have time, competence, context and authority to intervene.
lessons.case: A utility proposes an agent that summarizes sensor alarms and recommends maintenance. A later proposal would let it issue control commands to field devices. These are different risk classes. Advisory analytics can be piloted with read-only data and human review; direct control requires a separate hazard analysis, OT security assessment, fail-safe design and sector-specific approval.

lab.title: Create sector assurance profiles
lab.intro: Compare three fictional deployments: bank payment preparation, hospital discharge documentation and energy asset maintenance. Decide what autonomy is permissible, what must remain human-controlled and what evidence is required.
tasks: For each sector, identify safety, privacy, integrity, availability and accountability impacts.
Define read-only, draft, reversible-write and high-impact action boundaries.
Specify sector-specific approval, override, failover and recovery controls.
Identify dependencies and concentration risks, including cross-border hosting.
Create measurable acceptance criteria and a residual-risk decision.
lab.evidence: Three sector profiles, comparative autonomy matrix and assurance evidence checklist.
lab.model: The bank agent may prepare but not release payments; beneficiary changes and transfers require independent authorization. The hospital documentation agent may draft from authorized records but a qualified clinician verifies the content and owns the clinical decision. The energy agent remains read-only advisory in the proposed initial scope; any future command capability requires a separate safety case and OT architecture review. Each profile includes degraded-mode operation and manual fallback. Shared cloud dependencies are assessed for outage and geopolitical concentration risk.

lessons.title: Capstone: Design and Assure a Secure Agentic Enterprise
lessons.lead: Integrate threat modelling, identity, architecture, testing, governance and response into a defensible design.

slides.title: Capstone brief and system boundary

Capstone brief and system boundary

Core principle

Define a realistic enterprise workflow, stakeholders, business objectives, systems, users, data and external dependencies.

slides.html:
Business and security requirements

Core principle

Translate business outcomes into measurable requirements for confidentiality, integrity, availability, purpose and accountability.

Applied scenario

A requirement states that no refund above a defined threshold can commit without named approval.

Engineering response

Write acceptance criteria with measurable evidence and explicit negative cases.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Which requirement can be tested automatically at the backend?

slides.title: Asset and data inventory
slides.html:
Asset and data inventory

Engineering response

Which data asset has the highest combined confidentiality and integrity impact?

Agent and tool inventory

A malicious attachment attempts to trigger a refund through a delegated finance agent.

Identity and delegation design

Where is the final non-bypassable enforcement point?

Infrastructure and isolation plan

Assurance case and adversarial evaluation

Core principle

The claim that refunds are bounded is supported by backend checks, negative tests and sampled audit logs.

Final design review and defense

guide: The capstone integrates the course into a defensible engineering package. The scenario is a customer-operations platform with a research agent, case-management agent and bounded refund executor. The system reads customer messages and policy documents, retrieves case data, drafts responses, updates cases and may issue refunds under explicit conditions. Learners must define the scope, requirements, assets, data, identities, trust boundaries, threat model, architecture, policies, tests, monitoring, incident response and governance evidence.

A good design begins with constraints and measurable requirements, not a preferred framework. State what the system is allowed to do, what it is forbidden to do, what data it may access, what human decisions remain mandatory and what happens when dependencies fail. Translate requirements into enforceable controls and tests. A requirement such as ‘the agent must be secure’ is not testable. A requirement such as ‘no refund request commits unless the authenticated customer owns the case, the amount is within the approved limit, the grant is current and the approval is bound to the canonical transaction’ is testable.

The final assurance case should connect claims to arguments and evidence. Example claim: unauthorized refunds are prevented. Argument: the model cannot directly call the payment API; the execution service validates identity, scope, transaction state, limits and approval; the payment API rechecks authorization and idempotency. Evidence: architecture, policy tests, integration tests, adversarial results, logs and incident tabletop. Record assumptions and residual risks. The capstone is not complete if the controls exist only in diagrams or if tests do not exercise the actual enforcement points.
lessons.case: The organization wants to deploy the customer-operations platform in 90 days. Leadership asks for a defensible go/no-go recommendation. Your team must distinguish the minimum viable safe release from future capabilities. The first release may research and draft, with tightly bounded case updates; refunds remain behind independent approval until the execution path passes assurance tests.

lab.title: Capstone: design, test and defend a secure agentic enterprise
lab.intro: Produce a complete architecture and assurance pack for the customer-operations platform. Treat all systems, customers and transactions as fictional. Your final recommendation must state what can safely launch now, what must be deferred and what evidence is still missing.
tasks: Define system scope, stakeholders, business objectives, constraints and measurable security requirements.
Produce asset/data inventory, identity/delegation model, trust-boundary diagrams and threat register.
Design secure architecture with least agency, runtime policy enforcement and resource-side authorization.
Specify safe RAG/memory lifecycle, MCP/tool controls, sandbox, cloud guardrails and supply-chain evidence.
Create a risk-based test plan including long-horizon and multi-agent cases, monitoring and incident response.
Prepare governance pack, residual-risk register, implementation roadmap and go/no-go decision.
lab.evidence: A complete architecture dossier: context and deployment diagrams; data and identity maps; threat model; policy specification; test cases/results; monitoring and IR plans; supplier register; governance records; ADRs; residual-risk statement; and executive decision.
lab.model: A defensible minimum release keeps research and drafting separate from execution. The research agent has read-only access to approved sources; the case agent can draft updates but writes are checked by resource-side policy; the refund executor is a separate service with its own identity and strict transaction-bound approval. Retrieved content is provenance-tagged and cannot grant authority. Memory is tenant/case scoped. Tool schemas are pinned and reviewed. The runtime has no ambient cloud credentials and uses bounded execution. Tests measure actual side effects across multi-turn and cross-agent chains. The go/no-go decision defers any capability whose authorization, monitoring or recovery evidence is incomplete. A good answer names assumptions and does not claim zero risk.

quiz.q: What distinguishes a complete assurance case from a design presentation?
o: Claims are supported by explicit arguments and testable evidence.
quiz.why: Assurance links security claims to reasoning, controls and evidence.

quiz.q: What is the safest launch decision when refund authorization has not been tested?

glossary.def: Software system that uses a model and surrounding logic to pursue goals through context, tools and state.
The complete socio-technical system: model, host, orchestration, tools, identity, data, people and operations.
Granting bounded authority from one principal or component to another for a defined purpose.
Giving an agent the minimum capability, scope, duration and consequence required.
Untrusted content manipulates model behavior by being interpreted as instructions.
Prompt injection delivered through retrieved or tool-provided content rather than directly by the user.
Manipulation of tool metadata, schema, implementation or outputs to influence or misuse agent capability.
A privileged intermediary is induced to misuse its authority for a less-privileged caller.
Retrieval-augmented generation: retrieving external information to provide context to a model.
Persistent malicious or false content is written to memory and influences later tasks.
